title: Slipstream: nonlinear beam dynamics in PyTorch
summary: Slipstream is a PyTorch package for nonlinear beam dynamics in storage rings, linacs and photoinjectors. It provides CPU and GPU particle tracking, field-map injector models with space charge, and automatic differentiation along supported tracking paths. Comparisons with elegant, ASTRA, GPT and other codes assess accuracy and computational cost for nonlinear ring tracking, optics matching and photoinjectors. Ring tunes agree with elegant to $10^{-9}$. For the tested ring workloads with tens of thousands of particles, GPU tracking in float32 is hundreds of times faster than the single-threaded CPU implementations compared here. Automatic differentiation reduces the time for 24-parameter optics matching by an order of magnitude compared to finite differences. Using a high-brightness photo-injector as an example, final horizontal emittances agree with ASTRA to about 1% at 20 and 100pC and differ by $\approx$4% at 250pC. For $2^{18}$ macroparticles, Slipstream's faster default settings take 14s on an RTX 3050 GPU and give emittances within 2% of that of ASTRA. Additional tests examine coherent synchrotron radiation, dynamic aperture and resistive-wall impedance. The package was developed predominantly by AI coding assistants under human direction. These comparisons identify where its models, GPU execution and derivatives are useful for repeated simulations in scans, fits and optimisation.

AI.tldr: Slipstream is a PyTorch package for nonlinear beam dynamics in storage rings, linacs, and photoinjectors, offering CPU/GPU tracking, space-charge field-map injector models, and automatic differentiation. It is benchmarked against elegant, ASTRA, GPT, and other codes for accuracy and computational cost.

title: Toward light-controlled transverse Wigner ordering in attosecond electron beams
comment: 25 pages (13 pages main text including 3 figures, plus 12 pages Supplemental Material)
summary: Kinetic fluctuations and space-charge expansion hinder Wigner ordering in free-electron beams. Here we propose a laser-driven route toward transient, substrate-free Wigner ordering that combines photon-induced near-field electron microscopy (PINEM) attosecond bunching, synchronized magnetic focusing, and spatial preconditioning. Classical relaxation and zero-temperature fixed-node diffusion Monte Carlo trap benchmarks show that sixfold order survives quantum fluctuations from 1 T to sub-Tesla fields, defining ultrafast preparation targets.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a laser-driven, substrate-free route to transient transverse Wigner ordering in free-electron beams by combining PINEM attosecond bunching, synchronized magnetic focusing, and spatial preconditioning. Classical relaxation and zero-temperature fixed-node diffusion Monte Carlo benchmarks indicate that sixfold order survives quantum fluctuations from 1 T to sub-Tesla fields and define ultrafast preparation targets.
AI.motivation: Kinetic fluctuations and space-charge expansion hinder Wigner ordering in free-electron beams, motivating a transient, substrate-free preparation strategy.
AI.method: The proposed route combines photon-induced near-field electron microscopy (PINEM) attosecond bunching, synchronized magnetic focusing, and spatial preconditioning. The authors use classical relaxation and zero-temperature fixed-node diffusion Monte Carlo trap benchmarks to assess quantum fluctuations and define ultrafast preparation targets; experimental implementation details are not provided in the abstract.
AI.result: The benchmarks show that sixfold Wigner order survives quantum fluctuations for magnetic fields ranging from 1 T to sub-Tesla fields, thereby defining ultrafast preparation targets.
AI.conclusion: The proposed laser-driven combination is presented as a route toward transient, substrate-free transverse Wigner ordering in attosecond electron beams. The abstract reports theoretical and computational benchmarks rather than an experimental demonstration.

title: Electron versus positron impact ionization of inner shells of heavy atoms: distortion, exchange and relativistic effects
comment: 5 pages, 4 figures; numerical data in ancillary file
summary: Triple differential cross sections are presented for electron and positron impact ionization of the K shells of Cu, Ag, Au and U and the L shells of Ag. Relativistic effects are important throughout. For positrons the recoil maximum is suppressed and the recoil-region spin asymmetry changes sign; for the $2s$ shell the binary peak changes. In symmetric geometry, where theory reproduces the measured absolute electron cross section, the positron peak lies on the other side of zero recoil. Measurements would test relativistic ionization theory in a regime that electron experiments cannot reach.

AI.tldr: The paper presents triple differential cross sections for electron and positron impact ionization of inner shells of Cu, Ag, Au, and U and the L shells of Ag, showing that relativistic effects strongly affect the results and that positron measurements could test relativistic ionization theory in a regime inaccessible to electron experiments.
AI.motivation: The study aims to compare electron and positron impact ionization of inner shells of heavy atoms and to identify observable positron-specific signatures of relativistic effects, distortion, and exchange that could be tested experimentally where electron experiments cannot reach.
AI.method: Triple differential cross sections are presented for electron and positron impact ionization of the K shells of Cu, Ag, Au, and U and the L shells of Ag, with distortion, exchange, and relativistic effects considered.
AI.result: Relativistic effects are important throughout. For positrons, the recoil maximum is suppressed and the recoil-region spin asymmetry changes sign; for the 2s shell, the binary peak changes. In symmetric geometry, where theory reproduces the measured absolute electron cross section, the positron peak lies on the other side of zero recoil.
AI.conclusion: Measurements of positron-impact inner-shell ionization would test relativistic ionization theory in a regime that electron experiments cannot reach.

title: Probing the Rung-Mott Insulator in Bosonic Two-Leg Ladders
summary: Mott insulators typically appear at integer densities, but certain lattice geometries or non-local interactions can stabilise Mott insulators at fractional densities. In this work, we study strongly interacting two-leg ladders using ultracold bosonic atoms around half-filling, and identify the rung-Mott insulating (RMI) phase through its characteristic rung occupation in site-resolved measurements. We probe its excitation spectrum via lattice modulation spectroscopy, and interpret the observed spectra using numerical simulations that include the driven dynamics, coupling to multiple excited states, and energy offsets. As with other Mott insulators, the RMI phase is characterized through its incompressibility, which we probe via a site-resolved analysis of densities and chemical potentials. Our results provide direct insight into the excitation dynamics of a strongly correlated ladder system, and pave the way for studying transport and further dynamical properties in low-dimensional quantum systems with programmable lattice geometries.

AI.tldr: The paper studies strongly interacting ultracold bosons in two-leg ladders near half-filling, identifies a rung-Mott insulating phase using site-resolved rung occupation, probes its excitation spectrum with lattice modulation spectroscopy, and interprets the spectra with numerical simulations including driven dynamics, multiple excited states, and energy offsets. Incompressibility is characterized through site-resolved density and chemical-potential analysis.
AI.motivation: Mott insulators usually occur at integer densities, but specific lattice geometries or non-local interactions can stabilize Mott insulating phases at fractional densities. The work aims to directly probe the rung-Mott insulator and its excitation dynamics in a strongly correlated two-leg ladder system.
AI.method: Ultracold bosonic atoms are used in strongly interacting two-leg ladders around half-filling. The rung-Mott insulating phase is identified through its characteristic rung occupation in site-resolved measurements. Lattice modulation spectroscopy probes the excitation spectrum, and numerical simulations that include the driven dynamics, coupling to multiple excited states, and energy offsets are used to interpret the observed spectra. Incompressibility is probed via site-resolved analysis of densities and chemical potentials.
AI.result: The rung-Mott insulating phase is identified through its characteristic rung occupation and incompressibility in site-resolved measurements. Lattice modulation spectroscopy yields excitation spectra, which are interpreted using numerical simulations incorporating driven dynamics, multiple excited states, and energy offsets. No quantitative values or detailed spectral features are provided in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: The results provide direct insight into the excitation dynamics of a strongly correlated ladder system and pave the way for studying transport and further dynamical properties in low-dimensional quantum systems with programmable lattice geometries.

title: Perturbation of CO A1Π by a3Π should have been undetectable: detection, mechanism, and surprises
summary: A direct perturbation between the $a^3Π$ and $A^1Π$ vibrational levels of two electronic states that belong to the same electronic configuration of the carbon monoxide molecule should be unobservably weak because the vibrational overlap integral $\langle a^3Π,v' \mid A^1Π,v'' \rangle$ for their near-degenerate levels is extremely small. Yet level-shift and transition-intensity signatures of the $a^3Π(v = 13) \sim A^1Π(v = 2)$ perturbation are unmistakably present in the $^{13}\mathrm{C}^{18}\mathrm{O}$ isotopologue. A detailed study of, among others, the $A^1Π$ - $X^1Σ^+(2, 0)$, $B^1Σ^+$ - $A^1Π(0, 2)$, and $C^1Σ^+$ - $A^1Π(0, 2)$ spectra, obtained by the VUV- and Vis-FT complementary techniques in the energy regions of the six crossing points ($e$- and $f$-symmetry, $|Ω| = 0, 1, 2$) between the $a^3Π(v = 13)$ and $A^1Π(v = 2)$ states, reveal that the perturbation pathways are indirect, primarily facilitated by the $e^3Σ^-(v = 4)$ state, and that quantum mechanical interferences via its F1e and F3e components occur.

AI.tldr: Signatures of the nominally forbidden a3Π(v=13)–A1Π(v=2) perturbation in 13C18O were detected and shown to arise through indirect pathways, primarily involving e3Σ−(v=4), with quantum interference between its F1e and F3e components.
AI.motivation: A direct perturbation between the a3Π and A1Π levels, which belong to the same electronic configuration of carbon monoxide, was expected to be unobservably weak because the vibrational overlap integral for the near-degenerate levels is extremely small; nevertheless, level-shift and transition-intensity signatures are present, motivating a detailed investigation of their origin.
AI.method: The authors studied the A1Π–X1Σ+(2,0), B1Σ+–A1Π(0,2), and C1Σ+–A1Π(0,2) spectra, among others, using complementary VUV- and Vis-FT techniques in the energy regions of the six crossing points for e- and f-symmetry with |Ω| = 0, 1, and 2 between a3Π(v=13) and A1Π(v=2) in 13C18O.
AI.result: The perturbation is unmistakably present despite the extremely small direct vibrational overlap. The perturbation pathways are found to be indirect, primarily facilitated by the e3Σ−(v=4) state, and quantum mechanical interferences via its F1e and F3e components occur.
AI.conclusion: The a3Π(v=13)∼A1Π(v=2) perturbation, although expected to be undetectable from a direct-coupling perspective, is observable through indirect-state-mediated pathways and interference effects, with e3Σ−(v=4) playing the principal role.

title: Symmetry-constrained order hierarchy of connected optical responses in a five-level Rydberg-EIT medium
summary: Determining the connected many-body correlations required for a nonlinear optical response of a given order is a central challenge in interacting open quantum systems. We establish a symmetrybased selection rule for connected optical responses in a driven-dissipative Rydberg-EIT model. Under the specified Lindblad conditions, local phase covariance and zero-probe factorization imply that an n-atom connected contribution to the root optical coherence is forbidden below probe-amplitude order 2n-1. Consequently, optical-response coefficients through fifth order involve at most three-atom connected clusters, without assuming weak interatomic interactions. Direct finite-cluster calculations confirm the predicted lowest allowed orders, while an illustrative Maxwell-propagation calculation shows that triplet contributions can partially oppose pair-induced polarization rotation. Our results establish a rigorous connection between optical perturbation order and the connected many-body sectors that can contribute to it.

AI.tldr: The paper derives a symmetry-based order hierarchy for connected optical responses in a driven-dissipative five-level Rydberg-EIT medium, showing that an n-atom connected contribution first appears at probe-amplitude order 2n-1; finite-cluster calculations confirm the lowest allowed orders, and Maxwell propagation illustrates a competition between triplet and pair contributions.
AI.motivation: Determining which connected many-body correlations are required for a nonlinear optical response of a given order is a central challenge in interacting open quantum systems.
AI.method: The authors establish a symmetry-based selection rule for connected optical responses in a driven-dissipative Rydberg-EIT model. Under specified Lindblad conditions, local phase covariance and zero-probe factorization are used to derive order constraints. Direct finite-cluster calculations test the predicted lowest allowed orders, and an illustrative Maxwell-propagation calculation examines pair and triplet contributions.
AI.result: An n-atom connected contribution to the root optical coherence is forbidden below probe-amplitude order 2n-1. Consequently, optical-response coefficients through fifth order involve at most three-atom connected clusters, without assuming weak interatomic interactions. Finite-cluster calculations confirm the predicted lowest allowed orders, and the Maxwell-propagation calculation shows that triplet contributions can partially oppose pair-induced polarization rotation.
AI.conclusion: The results establish a rigorous connection between optical perturbation order and the connected many-body sectors that can contribute to it in the specified Rydberg-EIT setting.

title: First-principles phase diagram of monolayer CrS$_2$ polymorphs under biaxial strain and its sensitivity to the Hubbard U parameter
summary: In correlated two-dimensional magnets the balance between competing electronic and magnetic phases is often set by the strength of the on-site Coulomb interaction, so that the predicted ground state can hinge on a parameter that is not uniquely defined. Monolayer CrS$_2$ lies squarely in this regime, hosting several energetically close polymorphs whose character ranges from non-magnetic semiconducting to magnetically ordered metallic. We therefore investigate, using DFT$+U$ within the generalized gradient approximation, the structural, magnetic, and electronic properties of the 1H, 1T, 1T$'$, and 1T$''$ polymorphs of monolayer CrS$_2$ under varying Hubbard interactions ($U=0$--$8$~eV) and biaxial strain ($-10\%$ to $+10\%$). The 1T-derived structures remain metallic and magnetic throughout, with $U$ acting mainly as a spectral renormalization. The 1H phase behaves differently, passing from a non-magnetic semiconductor through an antiferromagnetic semiconducting regime before metallizing, so that the gap closes as $U$ increases while the local Cr moment grows monotonically. Biaxial tensile strain at fixed $U$ induces a similar sequence of transitions. Along both tuning pathways, the two inequivalent nearest-neighbor Cr--Cr exchange channels progressively separate and cross, with the parallel-spin channel becoming dominant, accompanied by a breathing-type bond disproportionation. Independent calculations with a localized-orbital implementation reproduce the overall evolution but yield shifted critical values of $U$ and of strain, demonstrating the robustness of the phase diagram while highlighting the implementation dependence of the transition thresholds.

AI.tldr: This DFT+U study maps the structural, magnetic, and electronic phase behavior of monolayer CrS2 polymorphs as functions of Hubbard U and biaxial strain, showing a robust but implementation-sensitive phase diagram.
AI.motivation: In correlated two-dimensional magnets, the predicted ground state can depend on the non-unique on-site Coulomb interaction U; monolayer CrS2 hosts several energetically close polymorphs spanning non-magnetic semiconducting to magnetically ordered metallic states.
AI.method: The authors use DFT+U within the generalized gradient approximation to study the 1H, 1T, 1T', and 1T'' polymorphs of monolayer CrS2 for U = 0–8 eV and biaxial strain from -10% to +10%, with independent calculations using a localized-orbital implementation.
AI.result: The 1T-derived structures remain metallic and magnetic, with U mainly acting as spectral renormalization. The 1H phase evolves from a non-magnetic semiconductor through an antiferromagnetic semiconducting regime to a metal as U increases, with the gap closing and the local Cr moment growing monotonically; tensile strain at fixed U induces a similar sequence. Both pathways show progressive separation and crossing of the two inequivalent nearest-neighbor Cr–Cr exchange channels, dominance of the parallel-spin channel, and breathing-type bond disproportionation. The localized-orbital implementation reproduces the overall evolution but gives shifted critical U and strain values.
AI.conclusion: The phase diagram is robust across implementations, but transition thresholds depend on the implementation; U and biaxial strain are the key tuning parameters for the coupled electronic and magnetic phases of monolayer CrS2.

title: Efficient spin-lattice dynamics and spin thermometry with machine-learned magnetic potentials
summary: In finite-temperature spin-lattice dynamics, conventional force-only spin thermometers fail for energies nonlinear in each spin, while the standard semi-implicit SIB integrator requires two model evaluations per step. Here we introduce a geometric-probe spin temperature that is exact for arbitrary high-order smooth Hamiltonians using first-order spin forces alone without Hessians, making it naturally suited for nonlinear many-body machine-learning (ML) magnetic potentials. Complementarily, our cached-field integrator (CFI) stays second-order accurate with a single model evaluation per step, about halving the time per step with ML potentials. Extensive benchmarks against Monte Carlo across analytic and ML systems confirm both exact thermometry and accurate thermodynamics.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a geometric-probe spin temperature that is exact for arbitrary high-order smooth Hamiltonians using only first-order spin forces, plus a cached-field integrator that is second-order accurate with one model evaluation per step. Benchmarks against Monte Carlo on analytic and machine-learned magnetic systems confirm exact thermometry and accurate thermodynamics, with roughly halved time per step for ML potentials.
AI.motivation: Finite-temperature spin-lattice dynamics requires reliable spin thermometry and efficient integration. Conventional force-only spin thermometers fail when energy is nonlinear in each spin, and the standard semi-implicit SIB integrator requires two model evaluations per step, which is costly for machine-learned magnetic potentials.
AI.method: The authors formulate a geometric-probe spin temperature that is exact for arbitrary high-order smooth Hamiltonians and uses first-order spin forces alone without Hessians. They also introduce a cached-field integrator (CFI) that remains second-order accurate with a single model evaluation per step. They benchmark both against Monte Carlo for analytic and machine-learned systems.
AI.result: The geometric-probe thermometer provides exact spin thermometry, and the cached-field integrator yields accurate thermodynamics while about halving the time per step with ML potentials. Extensive benchmarks against Monte Carlo across analytic and ML systems confirm both exact thermometry and accurate thermodynamics.
AI.conclusion: The proposed geometric-probe spin temperature and cached-field integrator enable efficient and accurate finite-temperature spin-lattice dynamics with nonlinear many-body machine-learned magnetic potentials.

title: Variance and Higher-Order Moments in Computational Fluctuating Hydrodynamics with Multiplicative Noise
summary: Fluctuating hydrodynamics (FHD) models mesoscopic fluid systems by augmenting classical conservation laws with stochastic flux terms governed by the fluctuation-dissipation theorem. While traditional validation of computational FHD (CFHD) algorithms focuses primarily on second-order central moments of equilibrium fluctuations, accurately resolving higher-order moments, such as skewness and kurtosis, is essential for evaluating non-linear functions of hydrodynamic fields. In this work, we analyze finite-volume CFHD discretizations to evaluate second-, third-, and fourth-order central moments of thermodynamic fluctuations. Using the one-dimensional stochastic heat equation, we demonstrate that incorporating multiplicative noise is necessary to recover the expected gamma distribution for temperature in the canonical ensemble, whereas additive noise models yield a Gaussian distribution that fails to capture non-zero skewness and excess kurtosis. We also derive analytical expressions for inherent modeling errors that persist in the limit of vanishing time step for a variety of boundary conditions. Furthermore, we introduce an improved formulation for Dirichlet boundary conditions that eliminates large boundary-adjacent errors in the third central moment present in traditional boundary treatments. We also examine higher-order temporal integration schemes, demonstrating that Stratonovich-based integrators, such as Heun's predictor-corrector method, can reduce these modeling errors. Finally, numerical simulations of the full compressible, stochastic Navier--Stokes equations confirm the generality and practical applicability of the findings obtained from the stochastic heat equation.

AI.tldr: Finite-volume computational fluctuating hydrodynamics is analyzed for second-, third-, and fourth-order fluctuation moments. Multiplicative noise is necessary to recover the expected gamma temperature distribution, while improved Dirichlet boundary treatments and Stratonovich-based integrators reduce persistent modeling errors; compressible stochastic Navier–Stokes simulations support the generality of the findings.
AI.motivation: Traditional validation of computational fluctuating hydrodynamics algorithms focuses mainly on second-order central moments of equilibrium fluctuations. Higher-order moments such as skewness and kurtosis are needed to evaluate nonlinear functions of hydrodynamic fields accurately.
AI.method: The paper analyzes finite-volume computational fluctuating hydrodynamics discretizations for second-, third-, and fourth-order central moments of thermodynamic fluctuations using the one-dimensional stochastic heat equation. It derives analytical expressions for modeling errors that persist as the time step vanishes under various boundary conditions, introduces an improved Dirichlet boundary formulation, examines higher-order temporal integration schemes including Heun's predictor-corrector method, and performs numerical simulations of the full compressible stochastic Navier–Stokes equations.
AI.result: Multiplicative noise is required to recover the expected gamma distribution for temperature in the canonical ensemble, whereas additive noise yields a Gaussian distribution that fails to capture nonzero skewness and excess kurtosis. Analytical modeling errors persist in the vanishing-time-step limit for several boundary conditions. The improved Dirichlet formulation eliminates large boundary-adjacent errors in the third central moment present in traditional treatments, and Stratonovich-based integrators such as Heun's predictor-corrector method can reduce modeling errors. Compressible stochastic Navier–Stokes simulations confirm the generality and practical applicability of the stochastic heat equation findings.
AI.conclusion: Computational fluctuating hydrodynamics should resolve higher-order moments and incorporate multiplicative noise to capture non-Gaussian equilibrium fluctuations. Improved Dirichlet boundary treatments and Stratonovich-based temporal integrators can reduce persistent modeling errors, and the findings extend from the stochastic heat equation to the full compressible stochastic Navier–Stokes equations.

title: Modeling of Chemically Reactive Gas Flows for Multi-Scale Problems
summary: Accurate modeling of chemical reactions plays a key role in the investigation of high-temperature flows. The Direct Simulation Monte Carlo (DSMC) method provides highly accurate solutions for such flows. However, its computational cost becomes prohibitive for low Knudsen regimes. Particle-based continuum methods employing the Bhatnagar-Gross-Krook (BGK) or Fokker-Planck approximations have gained increasing attention in recent years, improve computational efficiency in low-Knudsen regimes by modeling relaxation processes rather than binary collisions, while retaining the particle approach that enables straightforward coupling with DSMC. In the last years, different continuum-based models in the open-source particle code PICLas have been extended to simulate gas mixtures with internal energy modes. The present work focuses on modeling of chemically reactive gas mixtures in the Ellipsoidal Statistical BGK model. Model accuracy is assessed for two test cases of a reactive gases confined in a reservoir.

AI.tldr: The paper extends modeling of chemically reactive gas mixtures within the Ellipsoidal Statistical BGK continuum particle method in PICLas and assesses accuracy using two reservoir test cases with reactive gases.
AI.motivation: High-temperature reactive flows require accurate chemistry modeling, but DSMC is computationally prohibitive in low-Knudsen regimes; particle-based continuum methods such as BGK and Fokker-Planck approaches offer improved efficiency while retaining coupling with DSMC.
AI.method: The work formulates chemically reactive gas-mixture modeling in the Ellipsoidal Statistical BGK model, building on prior extension of continuum-based models in the open-source particle code PICLas to gas mixtures with internal energy modes. Accuracy is assessed for two test cases of reactive gases confined in a reservoir.
AI.result: The ESBGK reactive-gas model is assessed for two reservoir test cases. The abstract does not provide quantitative accuracy results or comparisons.
AI.conclusion: Chemically reactive gas-mixture modeling was implemented in the ESBGK framework, and its accuracy was evaluated for two confined reactive-gas cases; detailed performance and validation findings are not stated in the abstract.

title: Parametric neural-network wavefunctions across a bosonic phase transition
summary: We propose Boseformer, a universal attention-based neural-network architecture for representing the wavefunctions of particles with bosonic quantum statistics, including superfluid and crystal phases. The model is trained to generate the wavefunction as a function of a Hamiltonian parameter across the quantum phase transition between these phases. Once trained with variational Monte Carlo optimization, it can serve as a foundation model describing the phase transition without the need to retrain it for individual parameter values. We demonstrate our method on a system of two-dimensional bosons with $1/r^3$ repulsive interaction.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Boseformer, an attention-based neural-network architecture that represents bosonic wavefunctions and is trained as a function of a Hamiltonian parameter across a superfluid–crystal quantum phase transition, using variational Monte Carlo and demonstrated on two-dimensional bosons with 1/r^3 repulsion.
AI.motivation: The authors aim to provide a universal neural-network representation of wavefunctions for bosonic quantum statistics, including superfluid and crystal phases, and to avoid retraining the model separately for each Hamiltonian parameter value across a quantum phase transition.
AI.method: Boseformer is an attention-based neural-network architecture trained to generate the wavefunction as a function of a Hamiltonian parameter across the phase transition. It is optimized with variational Monte Carlo and used as a foundation model for the phase transition, demonstrated on a two-dimensional boson system with 1/r^3 repulsive interaction.
AI.result: The trained model can describe the phase transition without retraining for individual parameter values. The method is demonstrated on two-dimensional bosons with 1/r^3 repulsive interaction; the abstract does not report quantitative accuracy or benchmark results.
AI.conclusion: Boseformer provides a parametric neural-network wavefunction approach for bosonic systems across superfluid and crystal phases, functioning as a foundation model for the quantum phase transition in the demonstrated 1/r^3 interacting two-dimensional boson system.

title: From Fermions to Vortices: Microscopic Simulations of Phase Ordering in a d-Wave Superconductor
summary: Describing bath-induced superconducting phase ordering directly from a microscopic fermionic Hamiltonian remains a formidable challenge. Here we develop a microscopic framework for this problem using the recently introduced adiabatic variational principle (AVP) and demonstrate its application to a two-dimensional $d$-wave superconductor. The central construction maps evolving, spatially inhomogeneous bond-pairing fields onto constrained Bogoliubov-de Gennes states, with the associated Lagrange multipliers determining the thermodynamic driving forces. This enables dissipative evolution of the superconducting order while retaining its microscopic electronic structure, without assuming a phenomenological Ginzburg-Landau free-energy functional. Starting from disordered pairing configurations, we resolve the emergence of phase coherence through vortex-antivortex annihilation and the accompanying evolution of local electronic spectra. Vortex decay and dynamical scaling recover the characteristic kinetics of two-dimensional phase ordering, providing a nontrivial benchmark of the framework. The solver-independent AVP formulation opens a route to microscopic studies of dissipative ordering and metastability in superconductors with intertwined stripe and pair-density-wave orders.

AI.tldr: The paper develops an adiabatic variational principle (AVP) framework that maps inhomogeneous bond-pairing fields in a two-dimensional d-wave superconductor onto constrained Bogoliubov-de Gennes states, enabling microscopic simulation of dissipative phase ordering without a phenomenological Ginzburg-Landau functional. Simulations from disordered pairing configurations show phase coherence emerging through vortex-antivortex annihilation, with vortex decay and dynamical scaling recovering two-dimensional phase-ordering kinetics.
AI.motivation: Describing bath-induced superconducting phase ordering directly from a microscopic fermionic Hamiltonian is a formidable challenge, and existing approaches may rely on phenomenological Ginzburg-Landau free-energy functionals.
AI.method: The authors use the adiabatic variational principle to map evolving, spatially inhomogeneous bond-pairing fields onto constrained Bogoliubov-de Gennes states, with Lagrange multipliers determining thermodynamic driving forces. This permits dissipative evolution of the superconducting order while retaining the microscopic electronic structure, without assuming a phenomenological Ginzburg-Landau free-energy functional. Simulations start from disordered pairing configurations.
AI.result: The simulations resolve the emergence of phase coherence through vortex-antivortex annihilation and the accompanying evolution of local electronic spectra. Vortex decay and dynamical scaling recover the characteristic kinetics of two-dimensional phase ordering, providing a nontrivial benchmark of the framework.
AI.conclusion: The solver-independent AVP formulation opens a route to microscopic studies of dissipative ordering and metastability in superconductors with intertwined stripe and pair-density-wave orders.

title: Path-probability gradients for optimizing force fields against dynamical observables
comment: 20 pages, 6 figures; Supplementary Information (15 pages) included
summary: Machine learning force fields inherit the errors of the electronic-structure methods used to generate their training data, and refining them against experimental measurements provides a direct route beyond this limit. However, such refinement remains difficult for dynamical observables because differentiating chaotic molecular trajectories yields unstable gradients. Here, we introduce PathGrad, which differentiates Langevin path probabilities instead of the trajectories themselves. The resulting gradient estimator is accumulated on the fly from thermal noise and force derivatives, and its variance remains stable as the trajectory length increases. We validated the gradient estimator against finite-difference calculations and used it to fine-tune molten-copper and water potentials against experimental diffusion coefficients together with structural constraints. For water, jointly optimizing diffusion and the oxygen-oxygen radial distribution function also improves the predictions of shear viscosity and rotational relaxation, neither of which is included in the optimization objective. Alignment at a single temperature also improves the apparent activation energies of multiple dynamical observables, bringing their temperature dependences closer to experiments. Moreover, the optimized potential exhibits smaller force errors relative to an independent, higher-level quantum-chemical reference, indicating that alignment with experiments improves the fidelity of the potential energy surface beyond the fitted targets. PathGrad thus establishes a general framework for incorporating experimental observables directly into force field optimizations.

AI.tldr: PathGrad optimizes machine-learning force fields against dynamical experimental observables by differentiating Langevin path probabilities rather than unstable chaotic trajectories, and it improves diffusion, structural, viscosity, relaxation, and activation-energy predictions.
AI.motivation: Machine-learning force fields inherit errors from the electronic-structure data used for training. Refining them against experimental measurements can overcome this limitation, but optimization against dynamical observables is difficult because gradients through chaotic molecular trajectories are unstable.
AI.method: The authors introduce PathGrad, which differentiates Langevin path probabilities instead of individual trajectories. Its gradient estimator is accumulated on the fly from thermal noise and force derivatives, and its variance remains stable as trajectory length increases. The estimator was validated against finite-difference calculations and used to fine-tune molten-copper and water potentials against experimental diffusion coefficients with structural constraints.
AI.result: PathGrad successfully fine-tuned molten-copper and water potentials. For water, jointly optimizing diffusion and the oxygen-oxygen radial distribution function also improved shear viscosity and rotational relaxation predictions, although neither was in the objective. Alignment at one temperature improved apparent activation energies of multiple dynamical observables, bringing temperature dependences closer to experiment. The optimized potential also showed smaller force errors against an independent higher-level quantum-chemical reference.
AI.conclusion: PathGrad provides a general framework for incorporating experimental observables directly into force-field optimization. Experimental alignment can improve the fidelity of the potential energy surface beyond the fitted targets.

title: Packing the Bragg sphere: complete three-dimensional photonic band gaps at the refractive index of polymers (1.55)
summary: Complete 3D photonic band gaps have so far been found only at refractive-index contrasts of about 1.9 and above, reached by rod-connected diamond lattice structures. Reciprocal-space design of quasiperiodic structures recently achieved considerable emission attenuation at much lower contrasts [L. Maiwald et al., Adv. Optical Mater. 10, 2100785 (2022)]. Here we implement systematic search and reciprocal-space design of periodic 3D structures with complete band gaps, solving a discrete optimization problem on an integer lattice. A gap above a high band needs the strongest Fourier components of the dielectric close to the Bragg sphere of that band. Crystals with large cells, started from Fourier peaks at the vertices of a polyhedron on this sphere and optimized against densely refined band edges, open complete gaps down to an index contrast of 1.55, that of common polymers against air. A rational approximant of an icosidodecahedron gave the most efficient location of the Fourier peaks among the polyhedra tested. Numerical calculations confirm the gaps over a resolution series, with band edges searched over the whole Brillouin zone. The best designs are connected porous networks, suited to a microwave test with printed polymer. A rigorous bound, valid for any structure, does not exclude gaps at lower index, and the next rational approximants of the icosidodecahedron, whose Bragg zones match bands 576 and 2440 almost exactly, point to where gaps at even lower contrast may be sought.

title: Mixing and Preserving Properties of Non-van der Waals 2D Materials in Sandwich-like Heterostructures
summary: Heterostructure interfaces created by stacking two-dimensional (2D) materials outline an appealing route towards achieving advanced electronic and magnetic functionalities at the nanoscale. Employing ab initio density functional theory (DFT), we investigate two classes of such trilayer HSs: purely non-vdW assemblies and hybrid vdW/non-vdW/vdW stacks. We show that non-vdW sandwiches undergo pronounced geometric reconstruction forming chemically bonded interfaces with large absolute binding energies up to an order of magnitude larger than those of conventional vdW HSs. These strong interactions drive extensive electronic hybridization, band gap renormalization, and tunable interlayer magnetic coupling. In contrast, vdW encapsulation largely protects the intrinsic atomic and electronic structure of the non-vdW sheet from the environment , while enabling charge transfer doping of the vdW layers. Our results thus establish sandwich HSs a versatile interface design platform, spanning interaction regimes from weakly perturbed encapsulation to strongly interacting chemically bonded systems with emergent electronic and magnetic behavior.

title: Thermodynamics of complex crystals from a generalized mean-field bond model
comment: 16 pages, 8 figures, 2 tables. Code: https://github.com/raynol-dsouza/mean-field-bond-model (doi:10.5281/zenodo.24493341). Data: doi:10.5281/zenodo.24466123
summary: We extend our previously introduced mean-field bond model from unary fcc lattices to crystals with multiple chemical species and sublattices, accurately predicting finite-temperature thermodynamics without statistical sampling. Our generalization reformulates the model in terms of the Wyckoff positions of the crystal, representing each by one atom, and solving for the bond density of the reference bond of each of its neighbor shells. Bond-bond correlation functions are built from the zero-temperature force constants, allowing the deviation of every bond in the crystal to be expressed through linear functions of the reference bond of a shell. Thermodynamic self-consistency is enforced by requiring a single virial temperature for the whole crystal, and compatibility of average bond lengths with crystal volume. Model predictions are validated against molecular dynamics simulations of unary, binary, and ternary crystals using Morse-type bonding potentials, parametrized for each shell from the force constants of empirical interatomic potentials at several isotropic strains. In each case, the predicted bond densities and thermodynamics agree with the simulations to within their statistical uncertainty. title: Augmented Imaginary-Time Evolution of Neural Quantum States with Implicit Time Steps
summary: Finding the ground states of quantum many-body systems remains a central challenge in physics and quantum chemistry. Imaginary-time evolution (ITE) offers a natural, widely used route, but its convergence is typically asymptotic. Variational approaches restrict this evolution to parameterized manifolds, with neural quantum states (NQS) providing flexible representations commonly optimized via stochastic reconfiguration (SR). Their performance depends on the geometry of the variational manifold, the convergence properties of ITE, and the stability of finite-step explicit (forward) integrators. By exploiting local geometric information of the energy landscape, the recently introduced augmented imaginary-time evolution (AITE) can, in principle, reach the ground state in finite imaginary time. To exploit the accelerated convergence of AITE in NQS optimization, we first combine an implicit Euler step with Galerkin projection to derive an implicit SR scheme that permits large, stable steps and substantially outperforms conventional methods. We use it to formulate an implicit version of AITE and show that its acceleration persists under variational projection and finite-step integration with asymptotically quadratic convergence of the energy error. With finite sampling, implicit schemes yield consistent gains, and implicit AITE becomes increasingly advantageous.

They analyze its behavior under variational projection, finite-step integration, and finite sampling.

title: OMNI-P3x universal neural network potential for large-scale computational photochemistry workflows
summary: Computational photochemistry supports the design and understanding of new materials. Trained on both ground- and excited-state conformations, it performs complete computational photochemistry workflows with accuracy approaching TD-DFT. We demonstrate its practical applicability by screening a combinatorial library of 234,375 flavylium derivatives, where the pretrained model performs ground-state geometry optimization and predicts absorption properties without additional QM calculations. Following fine-tuning, we further screen 162,960 xanthene-based dyes, identifying new candidates for red, near-infrared and short-wavelength infrared emission. title: SPARK: Spectral Preconditioned Analytic Residual Kolmogorov Arnold Networks for incompressible Navier Stokes equations
comment: 68 pages, 16 figures, 12 tables, to be submitted to Journal of Computational Physics
summary: We propose Spectral Jet KAN (SJ-KAN) to reduce the cost of differentiation and the network complexity of Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) for the Navier-Stokes (NS) equations. The input coordinates are embedded through Chebyshev bases whose spatial derivatives are known in closed form, and all differentiation matrices are computed once for the collocation points before training. A single linear layer compresses the Chebyshev bases into a few latent features, and a single nonlinear Chebyshev Kolmogorov-Arnold Network (CKAN) layer maps these features to the physical variables. Because the basis derivatives are known in advance and the compression is linear, the spatial derivatives in the NS equations are carried through the network analytically by a fixed sequence of matrix products and elementwise operations. Automatic differentiation (AD) is used only in backpropagation, to compute the gradients of the loss with respect to the network weights. We examine three variants of SJ-KAN (JetKAN, JetKAN-F, JetKAN-H), which differ in how the output layer maps the latent features to the physical variables. All variants are tested on the Taylor-Green vortex and on the lid driven cavity at Reynolds numbers Re = 100, 1000, 5000 and 10,000. The results are compared with a KAN that uses AD (PIKAN) and with a standard PINN. The SJ-KAN variants reach comparable or better accuracy than both, with up to 47 times fewer parameters and up to 8.2 times faster training per epoch. SJ-KAN also solves the lid driven cavity flow at Re = 10,000 without any reference data and with fewer than 9,000 trainable parameters. title: Parton Physics in the Schwinger Model from Matrix Product States
summary: Parton distribution functions (PDFs) and light-cone distribution amplitudes (LCDAs) encode the non-perturbative structure of hadrons in terms of their partonic constituents. They are defined through matrix elements containing parton operators that are connected by a Wilson line along a light-front direction, which makes them difficult to access in Euclidean lattice calculations. We demonstrate how parton functions can be directly obtained in Minkowski space using the Hamiltonian framework. We compute fermion and antifermion PDFs, LCDAs, and decay constants of the vector meson in the Schwinger model for several fermion masses. States in Hilbert space are efficiently represented by tensor networks, with an expressivity that is systematically controlled by a bond dimension. The light-front Wilson line is implemented as a stepwise evolution on the lattice that alternates spatial shifts of an external charge with Trotterized time-evolution steps acting on a matrix product state. All systematic uncertainties are quantified by varying and extrapolating in the lattice spacing, volume, bond dimension, gauge-field truncation, and Trotter step width. The slow growth of the entanglement entropy makes moderate bond dimensions sufficient, which supports the feasibility of using tensor networks for computing light-front matrix elements in more general settings. We confirm that the computed distributions fulfill the expected normalizations, momentum sum rules, and symmetry properties.

title: Neural-operator acceleration of bidirectional phonon Boltzmann-Fourier coupling for multiscale heat transport in silicon fin arrays
summary: Localized heating in semiconductor devices can produce non-diffusive phonon transport near heat-generating regions, while heat spreading through the surrounding substrate remains well described by Fourier conduction. We present a hybrid framework that couples a pretrained neural operator for the phonon Boltzmann transport equation (BTE) within individual fins to a Fourier model of a shared substrate. To reduce the cost of repeated BTE solves across fin positions and coupling iterations, a DeepONet maps each fin's substrate-interface temperature and heating state to its temperature and heat-flux fields. The operator is trained on interface temperatures generated by a linearized proxy of the coupled problem, which avoids explicit training data collection from full coupled runs. An energy-balance penalty regularizes the learned operator, and a mixed finite-element formulation represents substrate heat flux in an H(div)-conforming space. The two models exchange temperature and normal heat flux through a non-overlapping Schwarz iteration with adaptive Aitken relaxation. We evaluate the framework on an idealized three-dimensional array of 100 silicon fins. For a held-out switching configuration, the neural-operator-Fourier solution differs from the direct BTE-Fourier reference by a maximum of 0.3 K in temperature and 0.6% in relative flux across all fins. Excluding the one-time substrate factorization, the coupled surrogate run takes about 50 s, compared with 2 h 28 min for direct coupling, a speedup of approximately 180x. Additional held-out switching patterns converge with the same trained operator. These results demonstrate neural-operator acceleration of bidirectional kinetic-continuum coupling for the tested geometry and material. This bidirectional strategy may extend to other multiscale materials problems coupling learned local neural models with continuum solvers.

title: Nonlinear non-modal stability and minimal perturbations in electroconvection driven by unipolar injection
comment: 41 pages, 16 figures. Supplementary code in the ancillary files. The following article has been submitted to Physics of Fluids. After it is published, it will be found at https://pubs.aip.org/aip/pof
summary: Electroconvection in a dielectric liquid subjected to unipolar charge injection is subcritical. Convection can be sustained well below the threshold of linear stability theory, and experiments report onset far below it. We use nonlinear non-modal optimization to determine the smallest charge perturbations that trigger convection below the linear threshold. The method, based on a direct--adjoint formulation of the full electrohydrodynamic equations, recovers the classical linear threshold in the limit of small amplitudes. At finite amplitude, the most dangerous perturbations are localized charge deficits rather than excesses, because a deficit relaxes more slowly under Coulomb repulsion. The minimal perturbation needed for transition grows from about 0.5% of the injected charge near the linear threshold to 3% at two thirds of it, where the convective branch ends, in agreement with direct numerical simulations. Near the critical amplitude, trajectories approach an unstable steady state, the edge state, that separates the basins of attraction of rest and convection and originates from the critical linear mode. The damped oscillatory modes involved in the growth of the optimal perturbations are transit-time modes of the ion drift. The convective mode is the first of them, made stationary by the coupling with the flow, which explains why the instability sets in as a steady motion. Small charge fluctuations can therefore lower the onset of electroconvection to about two thirds of the linear threshold, helping to explain the discrepancy between linear theory and experiments.

title: Effect of humidity and phase transition on turbulent diffusion of droplets and water vapour in atmospheric turbulent flows
summary: We investigate the effect of humidity on turbulent diffusion of droplets and water vapour in atmospheric turbulent flows taking into account the effect of phase transitions on turbulent transport. We find that the coefficients of turbulent diffusion of droplets and water vapour decrease with increase the turbulent Damköhler number (the ratio of turbulent time in the integral scale and phase transition time for condensation of water vapour), while the coefficients of the mutual turbulent diffusion that describe the turbulent cross effects increase with this parameter. For large turbulent Damköhler number, the coefficient of turbulent diffusion of droplets is strongly depleted when the evaporation of droplets is much faster than the condensation of water vapour. The obtained theoretical relationships are potentially useful in modelling applications in the atmospheric turbulence.

title: Emergent cloud patterns from stochastic jump models of parcel microphysics
summary: Warm clouds organize into bands, cells, and intricate wave networks, yet the dynamical mechanisms connecting these forms remain difficult to isolate. To bridge unresolved parcel microphysics and cloud organization, we formulate a spatial jump-process model of cloud-water and rain-water anomalies in an activated regime and analyze its mean-field closure. Eliminating fast supersaturation adjustment from droplet growth and vapor transport supplies a screened environmental kernel, which we couple to a cubic Stuart-Landau oscillatory law. Averaging over Poisson parcel episodes and closing third-order moments yields a pseudoparabolic Ginzburg--Landau equation (PGLE), whose mixed space--time derivative encodes dynamic inertia, slowing fine-scale relaxation. Unlike diffusive amplitude equations, the PGLE splits into a regularized nonlinear Schrödinger Hamiltonian sector and a pseudoparabolic Allen--Cahn gradient sector governed by a conserved Noether charge, alongside an open-system liquid-water budget separating conversion from vapor exchange, fallout, and triad-driven domain-mean oscillations. Exact stability criteria show how dynamic inertia and amplitude-dependent frequency shifts (twist) control modulational loss of synchrony and resonant cross-carrier sideband gain above a critical twist threshold. Numerical integrations show that increasing twist transforms undulatus-like bands into defect-rich asperitas-like waves via defect proliferation, while subcritical competition consolidates cellular patterns into rolls. Even without twist, random anomalies evolve into a persistent cellular exclusion scale and actinoform-like spiral arms, while 1D wave breakup reorganizes into a two-frequency combination-tone spectrum. The jump model identifies omitted fluctuation moments for calibration against large-eddy simulations.

title: A consistent generalised kinetic equation for damped ocean waves
summary: Contemporary spectral wave models, including those used in operational wave forecasts and in coupled earth system models, assume damping and non-linear wave energy exchange to be independent. Here, we critically examine this assumption. Starting from the equations of weakly non-linear waves, we rigorously derive a governing equation that consistently couples damping and non-linear interactions. This consistent generalised kinetic equation does not lead to an appreciable change in total wave--energy dissipation, but compared to the standard additive damping approach there is a noticeable difference in the distribution of energy among the wave frequencies. This effect is particularly important for weak damping, and is a consequence of a memory effect retained in model. Even stronger differences are observed when damping is allowed to depend on wave frequency, as is characteristic of many wave processes of growing interest such as the interaction with other components of the earth system, e.g. the cryosphere. Compared to the purely additive formulation, our new damped generalised kinetic equation has improved numerical stability characteristics. The formulation presented therefore provides a possible basis for future operational wave modelling. While our results are for ocean waves, the derived generalised kinetic equation can be applied to other weakly nonlinear dispersive systems where external damping (or forcing) applies.
