title: Elastic rebound in viscous fluid: an efficient rigid--elastic splitting with an asymptotic gap model
summary:
We formulate and test a model for an elastic body that falls under gravity onto the bottom of a container filled with a viscous incompressible fluid and rebounds without topological contact. The body is a rigid body plus a small, quasi-static elastic deformation, represented by a fixed compliance operator. In the near-contact patch, the thin fluid film is described by a Reynolds equation with cavitation. This allows the use of coarse meshes that need not resolve the gap, enabling efficient simulation. The film is coupled implicitly to the elastic surface displacement and to the rigid normal motion. The bulk fluid is coupled monolithically to the rigid body. For the axisymmetric case with vertical translation, the coupled step reduces exactly to a small dense nonlinear problem for the film pressure, with the bulk eliminated through a $2x2$ affine map.
  The model is implemented in NGSolve and compared with the experiments of Hagemeier et al. (2021) and the Eulerian FSI simulations of Wahl et al. (2021a). For a PTFE ball the approach agrees with the Eulerian FSI to 1\%. For a soft rubber ball (St $\approx 120$) the purely elastic model gives about three times the measured rebound. Material damping is the most important missing effect: a Kelvin--Voigt compliance with loss factor $\tanδ=0.6$ gives 4.0\,mm, against 4.4\,mm measured. A planar version of the model is compared with the recently published 2D benchmark of Corti et al. (2026).
  The radius of the film patch is the only numerical parameter of the splitting. It is fixed by one a-priori rule for all configurations, derived from a dry Hertz estimate of the approach, and the results depend only weakly on it.

AI.tldr: The paper develops and tests an efficient rigid–elastic splitting model for a body that rebounds from a container bottom through a thin viscous fluid film without topological contact, using a Reynolds cavitation model in the near-contact patch and monolithic coupling to the bulk fluid.
AI.motivation: To simulate elastic rebound in a viscous incompressible fluid efficiently without resolving the thin near-contact gap, while capturing the coupling between the thin film, elastic surface deformation, rigid normal motion, and bulk fluid.
AI.method: The body is modeled as a rigid body plus a small quasi-static elastic deformation represented by a fixed compliance operator. The near-contact thin film is described by a Reynolds equation with cavitation and coupled implicitly to the elastic surface displacement and rigid normal motion; the bulk fluid is coupled monolithically to the rigid body. For axisymmetric vertical translation, the coupled step reduces to a small dense nonlinear problem for film pressure, with the bulk eliminated via a 2x2 affine map. The model is implemented in NGSolve, with the film-patch radius fixed a priori from a dry Hertz estimate.
AI.result: For a PTFE ball, the approach agrees with Eulerian FSI simulations to 1%. For a soft rubber ball (St ≈ 120), the purely elastic model predicts about three times the measured rebound; a Kelvin–Voigt compliance with loss factor tanδ = 0.6 gives 4.0 mm versus 4.4 mm measured. A planar version is compared with the 2D benchmark of Corti et al. (2026), and results depend only weakly on the film-patch radius.
AI.conclusion: The rigid–elastic splitting with an asymptotic gap model enables efficient simulation of elastic rebound in a viscous fluid. Material damping is the most important missing effect for the soft rubber case, and the single a-priori film-patch-radius rule performs robustly across configurations.

title: Physics-informed neural networks for strong normal shocks in kinetic relaxation models and the hard-sphere Boltzmann equation
summary: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) for kinetic equations have mostly been applied near equilibrium and judged by density, velocity and temperature. Here a network trained on the kinetic equation alone, with no reference data in the loss, solves steady normal shock waves and is assessed in eight fields: density, velocity, temperature, heat flux, stress, a third-order moment and two fourth-order moments. The network corrects a mixture of the two end-state Maxwellians by an unbounded, signed factor with exact inflow; the loss, the residual in three norms with conservation terms, is minimised by Adam and a self-scaled quasi-Newton method with continuation in the Mach number. For the hard-sphere Boltzmann equation at Mach 8, in a comparison made once after reference-free tests, the largest relative $L^2$ difference from direct simulation Monte Carlo (DSMC) over the eight fields is 0.19 per cent; at Mach 10 it is 0.34 per cent. The distribution function itself agrees with the reference over six decades in velocity space. For the Bhatnagar--Gross--Krook (BGK) model, a blind prediction at Mach 50 gives density, velocity and temperature to about 0.1 per cent and exposes a loss of accuracy confined to the two fourth-order moments. Its origin is identified as a passive reduced distribution that carries little weight in the loss; with a larger weight on that distribution and a longer optimisation, both moments are within 3.2 per cent of the discrete-velocity solution up to Mach 70 and 7.1 per cent at Mach 100. The Shakhov model is solved to Mach 20 and a Rykov-type model of nitrogen to Mach 15.

AI.tldr: A reference-free physics-informed neural network solves steady strong normal shock waves in kinetic relaxation models and the hard-sphere Boltzmann equation, accurately reproducing eight macroscopic fields and the distribution function; a reduced-distribution weighting issue limits two fourth-order moments but is mitigated by reweighting and longer optimization.
AI.motivation: Physics-informed neural networks for kinetic equations have mostly been applied near equilibrium and evaluated only through density, velocity, and temperature. This work aims to solve strong normal shocks without reference data in the loss and to assess accuracy across higher-order moments and the distribution function.
AI.method: The network is trained on the kinetic equation alone, with no reference data in the loss. It represents the distribution as a mixture of the two end-state Maxwellians corrected by an unbounded signed factor with exact inflow. The loss uses the residual in three norms with conservation terms and is minimized by Adam plus a self-scaled quasi-Newton method with continuation in Mach number. The approach is applied to the hard-sphere Boltzmann equation, the Bhatnagar--Gross--Krook model, the Shakhov model, and a Rykov-type model of nitrogen, with assessment over eight fields.
AI.result: For the hard-sphere Boltzmann equation, after reference-free tests and a single comparison, the largest relative L2 difference from DSMC over eight fields is 0.19 per cent at Mach 8 and 0.34 per cent at Mach 10; the distribution function agrees over six decades in velocity space. For the BGK model, a blind Mach 50 prediction gives density, velocity, and temperature to about 0.1 per cent but shows reduced accuracy in the two fourth-order moments. This is attributed to a passive reduced distribution carrying little loss weight; with larger weight and longer optimization, both moments are within 3.2 per cent of the discrete-velocity solution up to Mach 70 and 7.1 per cent at Mach 100. The Shakhov model is solved to Mach 20 and the Rykov-type nitrogen model to Mach 15.
AI.conclusion: The results indicate that a kinetic-equation-trained PINN can solve strong normal shocks without reference data and can achieve high accuracy in macroscopic fields and the distribution function. The identified limitation in fourth-order moments is linked to loss weighting of a passive reduced distribution and is substantially reduced by increasing that weight and extending optimization.

title: Cavitation inception delayed by structured surface roughness
comment: 27 pages, 12 figures, 3 tables. Submitted to the Journal of Fluid Mechanics
summary: Cavitation inception over structured rough surfaces is investigated experimentally in the diverging section of a Venturi. The diverging wall carries laser-etched checkerboards of square cavities with roughness aspect ratios $0.03 \leq k/d \leq 0.72$, tested at a Reynolds number of 95 160. Inception cavitation numbers were measured together with high-speed shadowgraphs of the near-wall flow, from which upstream-migrating nuclei were tracked and vapor-masked velocity fields were obtained by optical flow. Smooth walls recessed by the etched volume served as a control. The roughness delays inception, most strongly at intermediate $k/d$, where the inception cavitation number falls from 4.07 on the smooth wall to 3.33-3.46, whereas the recessed walls show no delay. The supply of nuclei is similar on all surfaces, so the delay does not come from a lack of nuclei. Instead, the roughness changes the near-wall flow. For $0.08 \leq k/d \leq 0.444$, a mean reverse-flow layer forms along the wall beneath a lifted shear layer, and vapor at inception appears further from the throat and away from the wall. At $k/d = 0.72$ the flow reverses only intermittently and the delay is smaller. On all surfaces except $k/d = 0.08$, the local cavitation number at inception varies linearly with the near-wall fluctuation energy, consistent with nuclei activated by pressure excursions about 6-8 times the r.m.s. fluctuation. The roughness thus delays inception not by limiting the nuclei, but by weakening the near-wall fluctuations that reach them.

AI.tldr: Structured surface roughness on a Venturi wall delays cavitation inception, especially at intermediate roughness ratios, by weakening near-wall fluctuations that activate nuclei rather than by reducing nuclei supply.
AI.motivation: To determine whether structured surface roughness delays cavitation inception and whether any delay is caused by limited nuclei supply or by changes in the near-wall flow.
AI.method: Cavitation inception was studied experimentally in the diverging section of a Venturi using laser-etched checkerboards of square cavities with roughness aspect ratios 0.03 <= k/d <= 0.72 at a Reynolds number of 95,160. Inception cavitation numbers were measured with high-speed shadowgraphs; upstream-migrating nuclei were tracked, and vapor-masked velocity fields were obtained by optical flow. Smooth walls recessed by the etched volume served as controls.
AI.result: Roughness delayed inception, most strongly at intermediate k/d, where the inception cavitation number fell from 4.07 on the smooth wall to 3.33-3.46; recessed walls showed no delay. Nuclei supply was similar on all surfaces. For 0.08 <= k/d <= 0.444, a mean reverse-flow layer formed beneath a lifted shear layer, and inception vapor appeared farther from the throat and wall. At k/d = 0.72, reversal was intermittent and the delay was smaller. Except at k/d = 0.08, the local inception cavitation number varied linearly with near-wall fluctuation energy, consistent with nuclei activated by pressure excursions about 6-8 times the r.m.s. fluctuation.
AI.conclusion: The roughness delays cavitation inception not by limiting nuclei but by weakening the near-wall fluctuations that reach them.

title: Finite amplitude shape oscillations of magnetic microbubble under uniform magnetic field
summary: This study presents a theoretical model for the non-spherical oscillations of a lipid-encapsulated bubble infused with magnetic particles and subjected to a uniform magnetic field. Since the applied magnetic field is uniform, its gradient vanishes, making the existing weakly magnetic membrane theory inapplicable. To overcome this limitation, an alternative formulation that accounts for both the thinness and weak magnetic nature of the bubble shell is developed. Using this formulation, the induced magnetic field is calculated for a spherical bubble and incorporated into a Lagrangian framework for describing the non-spherical oscillations. The resulting governing equations for the radial and shape modes are then derived. The analysis shows that both the natural frequencies and exponential stability of the shape modes increase with increasing applied magnetic field. The frequency response of the shape modes shifts towards higher frequencies as the applied magnetic field is increased, consistent with the increase in their natural frequencies. Furthermore, finite-amplitude oscillations exhibit a period-doubling sequence and progressively transition towards chaotic behaviour with increasing magnetic field strength.

AI.tldr: A theoretical model is developed for non-spherical oscillations of a lipid-encapsulated magnetic microbubble in a uniform magnetic field, showing that increasing field strength raises shape-mode natural frequencies and stability and drives finite-amplitude oscillations from period doubling toward chaos.
AI.motivation: Existing weakly magnetic membrane theory is inapplicable because a uniform applied magnetic field has zero gradient, so a new formulation is needed for magnetic microbubble shape dynamics under such a field.
AI.method: The authors formulate an alternative model accounting for the thinness and weak magnetic nature of the bubble shell, calculate the induced magnetic field for a spherical bubble, incorporate it into a Lagrangian framework for non-spherical oscillations, and derive governing equations for radial and shape modes.
AI.result: Both natural frequencies and exponential stability of shape modes increase with applied magnetic field strength; the shape-mode frequency response shifts to higher frequencies; finite-amplitude oscillations exhibit period doubling and increasingly transition toward chaotic behavior as the magnetic field increases.
AI.conclusion: The proposed formulation overcomes the limitation of existing weakly magnetic membrane theory for uniform fields and shows that applied magnetic field strength substantially controls shape-mode frequencies, stability, frequency response, and nonlinear dynamical transitions of the magnetic microbubble.

title: Three-Dimensional Wake Reconstruction and Cross-Scale Transfer for Floating Offshore Wind Turbines via Physics-Informed Fourier Neural Operators
summary: Coupled surge-pitch motions drive unsteady vortex interactions and dynamic wake meandering behind floating offshore wind turbines, complicating three-dimensional wake reconstruction from limited measurements and transfer across turbine scales. Large-eddy simulations coupled with an actuator line model generate fixed and surge-pitch wakes at motion-based Strouhal numbers $St=fD/U_\infty$ of 0.2-0.6 (where $f$, $D$, and $U_\infty$ are the motion frequency, rotor diameter, and inflow velocity) for the National Renewable Energy Laboratory 5 MW ($D=126$ m) and International Energy Agency 22 MW ($D=284$ m) turbines. A physics-informed Fourier neural operator framework combines four-dimensional spectral convolutions with incompressible continuity and rotor-forced momentum-residual regularization to reconstruct three-dimensional unsteady wakes from two observation planes. Trained on the 5 MW fixed and $St=0.2$-$0.5$ cases, the framework recovers near-wake double-peak deficits, motion-driven wake expansion, and coherent vortices through $St=0.6$ (mean wake-center and half-width errors within 1.3% and 1.0% of $D$), while 10% planar sampling preserves near-dense accuracy (relative $L_2$ error 0.0689 versus 0.0684). Applying transfer learning from the 5 MW to the 22 MW turbine lowers the three-dimensional streamwise-velocity error at $St=0.6$ by 36% relative to zero-shot inference (0.1066 to 0.0682), halves scratch-training error with one fixed case (0.0835 versus 0.1693), and restores wake-center tracking and motion-locked harmonics ($St$-$3St$). Large-scale motion-induced dynamics transfer cleanly across turbine scales, whereas fine-scale vortex breakdown remains damped. The framework shows potential for three-dimensional wake reconstruction and downstream-inflow assessment in floating wind farms.

AI.tldr: A physics-informed Fourier neural operator reconstructs three-dimensional unsteady wakes of floating offshore wind turbines from two observation planes and transfers wake dynamics from a 5 MW to a 22 MW turbine, preserving large-scale motion-induced dynamics while damping fine-scale vortex breakdown.
AI.motivation: Coupled surge-pitch motions produce unsteady vortex interactions and dynamic wake meandering behind floating offshore wind turbines, making three-dimensional wake reconstruction from limited measurements and cross-turbine-scale transfer difficult; the work is motivated by downstream-inflow assessment in floating wind farms.
AI.method: Large-eddy simulations coupled with an actuator line model generate fixed and surge-pitch wakes at motion-based Strouhal numbers of 0.2–0.6 for the National Renewable Energy Laboratory 5 MW and International Energy Agency 22 MW turbines. A physics-informed Fourier neural operator combines four-dimensional spectral convolutions with incompressible-continuity and rotor-forced momentum-residual regularization to reconstruct three-dimensional unsteady wakes from two observation planes; it is trained on 5 MW fixed and St=0.2–0.5 cases, evaluated through St=0.6 and under 10% planar sampling, and transferred to the 22 MW turbine.
AI.result: The framework recovers near-wake double-peak deficits, motion-driven wake expansion, and coherent vortices through St=0.6, with mean wake-center and half-width errors within 1.3% and 1.0% of rotor diameter D. With 10% planar sampling, relative L2 error is 0.0689 versus 0.0684 for near-dense sampling. Transfer learning from 5 MW to 22 MW reduces three-dimensional streamwise-velocity error at St=0.6 by 36% relative to zero-shot inference (0.1066 to 0.0682), halves scratch-training error with one fixed case (0.0835 versus 0.1693), and restores wake-center tracking and motion-locked harmonics from St to 3St; fine-scale vortex breakdown remains damped.
AI.conclusion: Large-scale motion-induced wake dynamics transfer cleanly across turbine scales, whereas fine-scale vortex breakdown remains damped. The framework shows potential for three-dimensional wake reconstruction and downstream-inflow assessment in floating wind farms.

title: Beyond the quasi-steady approximation: Modeling unsteady flows from steady solution families
summary: Many flow systems have well-established steady-state relations, but applying them quasi-steadily under unsteady forcing neglects memory effects. This study develops a modeling framework extending steady-state relations to unsteady flows by closing dynamic departures from the instantaneous steady state. Integral conservation laws determine the explicit balance structure, while finite-order temporal closures approximate unresolved spatial dynamics responsible for the memory effect. This formulation preserves the prescribed nonlinear steady-state relations as equilibria under constant forcing. Canonical benchmarks in laminar and turbulent channel flows and shallow-water wave propagation demonstrate that the required temporal structure depends on spatial memory and forcing timescale. First-order relaxation captures viscous diffusion, whereas wave propagation and boundary reflections require higher-order models for oscillatory memory. Modal analysis further reveals that the required dynamic resolution depends on the predicted quantity, with wall shear being more sensitive to higher viscous modes than bulk flow rate. Nonlinear extensions with state-dependent steady relations and dynamic coefficients reproduce transient lag, relaxation, and oscillations under slow-to-moderate forcing, including finite-amplitude regimes. However, rapid finite-amplitude waves expose the limits of locally linearized closures in capturing nonlinear phase dynamics. This framework compactly extends quasi-steady approximations while preserving exact steady-state consistency.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a modeling framework that extends prescribed steady-state flow relations to unsteady flows by closing dynamic departures from the instantaneous steady state, thereby accounting for memory effects while preserving exact steady-state consistency. Benchmarks show that the required temporal closure order depends on spatial memory, forcing timescale, and predicted quantity, with limitations for rapid finite-amplitude waves.
AI.motivation: Many flow systems have well-established steady-state relations, but applying them quasi-steadily under unsteady forcing neglects memory effects. The study aims to model unsteady departures from steady-state behavior without losing exact steady-state consistency.
AI.method: Integral conservation laws are used to determine the explicit balance structure, and finite-order temporal closures approximate unresolved spatial dynamics responsible for memory effects. The formulation preserves nonlinear steady-state relations as equilibria under constant forcing. It is assessed using canonical benchmarks in laminar and turbulent channel flows and shallow-water wave propagation, including modal analysis and nonlinear extensions with state-dependent steady relations and dynamic coefficients.
AI.result: First-order relaxation captured viscous diffusion, whereas wave propagation and boundary reflections required higher-order models for oscillatory memory. Modal analysis showed that wall shear is more sensitive to higher viscous modes than bulk flow rate. Nonlinear extensions reproduced transient lag, relaxation, and oscillations under slow-to-moderate forcing, including finite-amplitude regimes. Rapid finite-amplitude waves exposed limits of locally linearized closures in capturing nonlinear phase dynamics. No quantitative error metrics or parameter ranges are provided in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: The framework compactly extends quasi-steady approximations while preserving exact steady-state consistency. The required dynamic resolution depends on spatial memory, forcing timescale, and the predicted quantity, and locally linearized closures are insufficient for rapid finite-amplitude nonlinear phase dynamics.

title: Uncertainty Quantification and Global Sensitivity Analysis of Patient-Specific Coronary Hemodynamics Under Unsteady Flow Conditions
summary: Patient-specific computational models of the coronary arteries demonstrate transformative potential for physiological assessment, identifying hemodynamic markers associated with disease progression, and optimizing treatment. Unfortunately, these models rarely account for input parameter uncertainty, limiting confidence in predictions and their clinical interpretation. Herein, we present a novel uncertainty quantification-finite element framework that integrates computationally efficient techniques to characterize and propagate uncertainty through patient-specific coronary simulations under unsteady flow conditions. Principal component analysis characterized variability in pulsatile coronary velocity waveforms, while uncertainty in blood pressure, viscosity, density, and heart rate is represented through probability distributions. Polynomial chaos expansion (PCE) enabled efficient uncertainty propagation and global sensitivity analysis across three patient-specific models, quantifying variability in time-averaged wall shear stress (WSS), oscillatory shear index, and cross-flow index. Fourth-order PCE emulators converged across all three patients, yielding analyses of 505 models per patient, with median coefficients of variation ranging from 0.15-0.20 for time-averaged WSS, 0.54-0.75 for oscillatory shear index, and 0.28-0.38 for cross-flow index, highlighting greater relative uncertainty in multidirectional WSS metrics. Global sensitivity analysis revealed that time-averaged WSS variability was governed by the individual effects of velocity and blood viscosity, with parameter interactions contributing <2% of total variance. In contrast, velocity waveform uncertainty dominated variability in the oscillatory shear index and cross-flow index, with higher-order parameter interactions accounting for 20.7-34.5% and 26.6-37.8% of total variance, respectively.

AI.tldr: A finite-element uncertainty quantification framework using principal component analysis and polynomial chaos expansion quantified input uncertainty in patient-specific coronary hemodynamics, showing greater relative uncertainty and interaction effects for multidirectional wall shear stress metrics than for time-averaged wall shear stress.
AI.motivation: Patient-specific computational models of the coronary arteries can support physiological assessment, identify hemodynamic markers of disease progression, and optimize treatment, but they rarely account for input parameter uncertainty, which limits confidence in predictions and their clinical interpretation.
AI.method: The authors developed an uncertainty quantification–finite element framework for patient-specific coronary simulations under unsteady flow conditions. Principal component analysis characterized variability in pulsatile coronary velocity waveforms; blood pressure, viscosity, density, and heart rate uncertainty was represented by probability distributions; and polynomial chaos expansion was used for efficient uncertainty propagation and global sensitivity analysis across three patient-specific models, quantifying time-averaged wall shear stress, oscillatory shear index, and cross-flow index.
AI.result: Fourth-order polynomial chaos expansion emulators converged for all three patients, enabling analysis of 505 models per patient. Median coefficients of variation ranged from 0.15–0.20 for time-averaged wall shear stress, 0.54–0.75 for oscillatory shear index, and 0.28–0.38 for cross-flow index. Time-averaged wall shear stress variability was governed by individual effects of velocity and blood viscosity, with parameter interactions contributing less than 2% of total variance. Velocity waveform uncertainty dominated oscillatory shear index and cross-flow index variability, with higher-order parameter interactions accounting for 20.7–34.5% and 26.6–37.8% of total variance, respectively.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework efficiently characterizes and propagates uncertainty in patient-specific coronary hemodynamics and provides global sensitivity analysis. The results indicate greater relative uncertainty and stronger higher-order interaction effects for multidirectional wall shear stress metrics than for time-averaged wall shear stress, supporting more informed interpretation of computational predictions.

title: Self-arresting vortex rearrangements in pinned spinning-down superfluids
comment: 9 pages, 3 tables, 3 figures, 3 animations. To be submitted to PRL
summary: Superfluids, in a spinning-down container with pinning centres, exhibit sudden collective migration of quantized vortices. The onset, progress, and termination of this process remain poorly understood. Here, we show that: 1) the first exodus of vortices occurs when a sector of the vortex array, having a minimum opening angle, is vacated close to the wall; 2) driven by this exodus, the superfluid flow near the boundary continually decreases in strength and arrests the exit; and 3) the resultant depletion region has well-defined dimensions---governed primarily by the critical unpinning velocity, the container size, and the initial rotation rate---that limit the angular momentum transferred to the container. We conclude by discussing the relevance to pulsar glitches.

AI.tldr: The paper explains self-arresting collective vortex rearrangements in a pinned spinning-down superfluid: vortex exodus begins when a near-wall sector is vacated, boundary flow weakens and stops the exit, and the resulting depletion region limits angular momentum transfer; relevance to pulsar glitches is discussed.
AI.motivation: The onset, progression, and termination of sudden collective migration of quantized vortices in a spinning-down superfluid with pinning centres are poorly understood, motivating a mechanism that may also relate to pulsar glitches.
AI.method: The abstract does not provide methodological details. It reports a theoretical/analytical account showing three features of the rearrangement process: the condition for the first vortex exodus, the feedback that arrests vortex exit, and the scaling of the depletion region.
AI.result: The first exodus occurs when a sector of the vortex array, with a minimum opening angle, is vacated close to the wall. This exodus continually weakens the superfluid flow near the boundary and arrests the exit. The resulting depletion region has well-defined dimensions governed primarily by the critical unpinning velocity, container size, and initial rotation rate, limiting the angular momentum transferred to the container.
AI.conclusion: The vortex rearrangement is self-arresting, with its onset and termination controlled by near-wall vortex-array vacancy, boundary-flow feedback, and depletion-region dimensions. The authors discuss the relevance of this mechanism to pulsar glitches.

title: Quantum-Inspired Tensor Train Spectral Solver for High-Resolution PDEs with Non-Periodic Boundary Conditions
summary: Tensor train (TT) methods enable high-resolution computational mechanics simulations by exploiting low-rank structure in discretized fields and operators. While the superfast Fourier transform (SFFT) has enabled efficient TT-based spectral solvers for periodic problems, corresponding representations for non-periodic boundary conditions remain underexplored. We introduce the superfast cosine and sine transforms (SFCT and SFST), extending the TT spectral framework to homogeneous Neumann and Dirichlet boundary conditions, respectively. Building on a quantum-circuit construction of the discrete cosine and sine transforms, we derive both transforms from a shared TT operator representation and prove that their TT ranks are bounded by $6r_S$, independently of the discretization order, where $r_S$ is the rank of the SFFT at the prescribed accuracy. The measured ranks plateau near 32 for grid sizes up to $2^{26}$ points. For Rayleigh-Bénard convection, spectral pressure projection achieves up to a 7-fold speedup in the Poisson solve relative to a preconditioned physical-space TT solver while maintaining comparable accuracy. Three-dimensional computational homogenization achieves a 2-6-fold speedup and a 4-7-fold reduction in memory consumption compared with the existing TT-based approach. The results establish an efficient TT framework for spectral PDE solvers with non-periodic boundary conditions.

AI.tldr: The paper extends tensor-train spectral PDE solvers from periodic domains to homogeneous Dirichlet and Neumann boundary conditions by introducing superfast cosine and sine transforms with bounded TT ranks, and demonstrates speed and memory gains in convection and homogenization problems.
AI.motivation: Tensor-train methods enable high-resolution computational mechanics by exploiting low-rank discretized fields and operators, but efficient TT-based spectral solvers have mainly been available for periodic problems via the superfast Fourier transform; non-periodic boundary conditions remain underexplored.
AI.method: The authors introduce the superfast cosine transform and superfast sine transform for homogeneous Neumann and Dirichlet conditions, respectively. Using a quantum-circuit construction of discrete cosine and sine transforms, they derive both transforms from a shared TT operator representation and prove TT ranks bounded by 6r_S, independent of discretization order, where r_S is the SFFT rank at the prescribed accuracy.
AI.result: Measured TT ranks plateau near 32 for grids up to 2^26 points. For Rayleigh-Bénard convection, spectral pressure projection achieves up to a 7-fold speedup in the Poisson solve versus a preconditioned physical-space TT solver with comparable accuracy. Three-dimensional computational homogenization achieves 2-6-fold speedup and 4-7-fold memory reduction compared with the existing TT-based approach.
AI.conclusion: The results establish an efficient tensor-train framework for spectral PDE solvers with non-periodic boundary conditions.

title: Impact of Taylor-Aris dispersion on chemical patterns in confined channel flows
summary: Chemical patterns form through non-linear interactions between different species. We study how confined channel flows affect pattern formation using the Brusselator as a paradigmatic activator-inhibitor model. An invariant-manifold method for slender channels reduces the advection-diffusion-reaction equation to one spatial dimension, with species transported at the mean flow velocity and molecular diffusivities replaced by the classical Taylor-Aris dispersion coefficients. We obtain the phase diagram as a function of the Péclet number (i.e., the relative strength of advection to diffusion), the channel slenderness, and the diffusivity ratio of the species. Our analytical results demonstrate that the classical Turing criterion can become inverted at large Péclet numbers and, thus, channel flow can trigger pattern formation even when the molecular diffusivities violate the classical Turing condition, and conversely destroy pre-existing patterns. Both predictions are confirmed by direct numerical simulations, which show advected stripe patterns, whose wavelength can be predicted by our reduced theory, as well as oscillatory dynamics. These findings highlight that hydrodynamic flows can modify chemical mixing and thereby profoundly affect pattern formation in channel geometries.

AI.tldr: A one-dimensional reduction using Taylor-Aris dispersion shows that confined channel flow can invert the classical Turing criterion, triggering or destroying chemical patterns depending on Péclet number, channel slenderness, and species diffusivity ratio; direct simulations confirm advected stripes and oscillatory dynamics.
AI.motivation: The paper aims to understand how confined channel flows and hydrodynamic transport modify chemical pattern formation, particularly whether flow-induced Taylor-Aris dispersion can alter the classical Turing instability condition for activator-inhibitor systems.
AI.method: The authors use the Brusselator as a paradigmatic activator-inhibitor model and apply an invariant-manifold method for slender channels to reduce the advection-diffusion-reaction equation to one spatial dimension. Species are transported at the mean flow velocity, and molecular diffusivities are replaced by classical Taylor-Aris dispersion coefficients. They derive a phase diagram as a function of Péclet number, channel slenderness, and species diffusivity ratio, and confirm predictions with direct numerical simulations.
AI.result: Analytical results show that the classical Turing criterion can become inverted at large Péclet numbers: channel flow can trigger pattern formation even when molecular diffusivities violate the classical Turing condition, and can conversely destroy pre-existing patterns. Direct numerical simulations confirm both predictions and show advected stripe patterns, whose wavelength is predicted by the reduced theory, as well as oscillatory dynamics.
AI.conclusion: Hydrodynamic flows can modify chemical mixing and thereby profoundly affect pattern formation in channel geometries. The abstract does not provide experimental validation or specific parameter values.

title: Saddle-focus to saddle transition of 4D heteroclinic orbits resembling oscillatory and regularized shock waves of some dissipative Boussinesq systems
summary: Oscillatory and regularized shock waves have long been studied to understand the formation and dynamics of undular bores in shallow waters, phenomena that typically arise from the interplay between dispersion, nonlinearity, and dissipation. In this work, we investigate and describe the nature and shape of traveling wave solutions that resemble oscillatory and regularized shock waves of some Boussinesq-type water wave models known as Bona--Smith systems in the presence of dissipation. The associated traveling wave equations are solutions of four-dimensional dynamical systems, leading to both computational challenges and rich structural behavior. In particular, to describe the properties of these traveling waves, we analyze heteroclinic orbits that connect two distinct equilibria, one of which undergoes a transition in the four-dimensional phase space from a saddle-focus to a saddle point as the dissipation parameter increases. This transition governs the nature of the wave profile, which evolves smoothly from an oscillatory shock wave to a regularized (non-oscillatory) shock wave. To compute such solutions, we introduce a finite-difference-based numerical method tailored for this class of problems.

AI.tldr: The paper studies traveling-wave solutions of dissipative Bona--Smith/Boussinesq-type water-wave models by analyzing four-dimensional heteroclinic orbits whose equilibrium changes from saddle-focus to saddle as dissipation increases, causing a smooth transition from oscillatory to regularized non-oscillatory shock profiles; a tailored finite-difference method is introduced for computation.
AI.motivation: Oscillatory and regularized shock waves are relevant to the formation and dynamics of undular bores in shallow waters, which arise from dispersion, nonlinearity, and dissipation. The authors aim to describe the nature and shape of traveling waves resembling such shock waves in dissipative Bona--Smith systems.
AI.method: The traveling-wave equations are treated as four-dimensional dynamical systems. The authors analyze heteroclinic orbits connecting two distinct equilibria, one of which transitions from a saddle-focus to a saddle as the dissipation parameter increases. They also introduce a finite-difference-based numerical method tailored to this class of problems.
AI.result: The saddle-focus-to-saddle transition governs the wave profile: the solution evolves smoothly from an oscillatory shock wave to a regularized, non-oscillatory shock wave as dissipation increases. The four-dimensional setting produces computational challenges and rich structural behavior; no quantitative parameter values or error measures are provided in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: The heteroclinic-orbit analysis links the equilibrium transition in the four-dimensional phase space to the qualitative change between oscillatory and regularized shock waves in dissipative Bona--Smith systems, and the proposed finite-difference method is designed to compute such solutions.

title: Critical ocean physics on the edge of AMOC instability
summary: The Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC) is expected to weaken under global warming, but whether this signifies a transient response or a tipping transition remains unclear. Distinguishing between these cases requires a physical understanding of the boundary separating ocean states leading to AMOC recovery from those leading to collapse. In a global ocean model with 1° resolution, we compute an AMOC edge state -- an unstable saddle equilibrium that anchors this instability boundary. The edge state maintains weak overturning sourced by marginal deep water formation in the Nordic Seas. Analyzing the North Atlantic freshwater and heat balances that govern the edge state dynamics, we show that near the edge state, thermal and haline components of the surface buoyancy flux approximately compensate. title: InletScope: Multiscale pressure-based inlet unstart monitoring under changing sensor configurations
summary: Supersonic inlets capture and compress air for aeroengines, and unstart can disrupt the air supply and compromise propulsion-system stability. title: Integrated lasing and dual-band gain in neodymium-implanted silicon nitride
summary: Lasers at wavelengths near 1 micrometer are used in quantum technologies, precision metrology, and sensing. Rare-earth gain at these wavelengths in photonic integrated circuits can reduce the size and enable the scalable fabrication of these lasers. The photonic integrated circuits were fabricated on a 200 mm commercial wafer platform, and individual dies were implanted with neodymium ions. We show that the amplifiers provide gain in two bands around wavelengths of 920 nm and 1100 nm, and we show lasing in a ring resonator. This demonstrates that neodymium-implanted LPCVD silicon nitride is a suitable gain material for integrated lasers.

title: Recipe for near-unity efficient frequency conversion via transient molecular modulation
summary: Frequency transduction technologies are an essential element for interfacing devices operating at distinct spectral regions. Specifically, the conversion of weak signals between different wavelengths is a fundamental requirement of quantum networks, where conversion efficiency is critical for preserving the statistical properties of light. In this regard, molecular modulation in gas-filled hollow-core fibers offers a promising approach for highly-tunable linear frequency conversion of classical and quantum light. However, recent experimental studies in this subject have struggled to overcome a saturation in conversion efficiency to about 70%, which, although high, might impair the faithful transfer of quantum properties upon conversion. In this work, we discuss a route to surpass this limitation that identifies the key factors to consider for obtaining quantum efficiencies exceeding 99%. These results might pave the way to viable fiber-based quantum transduction schemes for next-generation quantum networks.

title: Heat Reduction in Erbium-Doped Microresonator
summary: We investigate anti-Stokes fluorescence in a 106-micrometer-diameter silica whispering-gallery-mode microresonator coated with erbium-doped sol-gel, assessing its potential for reduced optical heating. Measurements over a temperature range of 25 to 62 degrees Celsius show that the mean fluorescence photon energy increases with externally controlled temperature. The measured pump-wavelength dependence is consistent with an absorption-weighted spectral model, which predicts an optimum near 1562.65 nm for the investigated spectral figure of merit. Resonance-dependent emission patterns further motivate a dual-frequency pumping scheme using two higher-order whispering-gallery modes. Calculated time-averaged field profiles indicate that complementary modal distributions can provide more uniform excitation near the equator. These results characterize spectral conditions relevant to fluorescence-based heat reduction and suggest a route toward improved spatial pump coverage. Demonstrating net optical refrigeration requires additional measurements of absorbed pump power and an independent thermal readout.

title: AI-Assisted Topological High-Harmonic Spectroscopy for Characterizing Crystal Symmetries and Nonlinear Responses
summary: Structured light has emerged as a unique tool for probing nonlinear light-matter interactions. Particularly interesting is its interaction with anisotropic media, such as crystalline materials, whose anisotropic responses encode information about their electronic properties. Recently, topological high-harmonic spectroscopy was introduced as an all-optical approach to extract the anisotropic nonlinear response of graphene from harmonic spatial intensity profiles. Here, topological high-harmonic spectroscopy is combined with artificial intelligence (AI) to retrieve the anisotropic non-linear response and crystal symmetry of atomically thin materials. A convolutional neural network is trained and validated to learn the inverse mapping between harmonic far-field intensity profiles and the nonlinear response of materials exhibiting different rotational symmetries. Comparisons with microscopic high-harmonic-generation simulations demonstrate the accurate retrieval of distinct effective nonlinear responses in single-symmetry crystals, such as single-layer graphene and bilayer graphene with different stacking orders, and in crystals exhibiting multiple symmetry components, such as monolayer hexagonal boron nitride. Macroscopic high-harmonic-generation simulations assess the robustness and applicability limits of the technique. These results establish AI-assisted topological high-harmonic spectroscopy as a fast, contactless tool for characterizing nonlinear optical responses and crystal symmetries without phase-resolved measurements, opening prospects for applications to complex systems such as polycrystals and van der Waals heterostructures.

title: Nonreciprocal state-selective splitting of eigenstates at a polarization exceptional point
summary: Non-Hermitian photonic systems can be engineered to exhibit exceptional points (EPs), where eigenvalues and eigenstates coalesce. Although perturbations near EPs have mainly been characterized through eigenvalue splitting, the branch-resolved evolution of the coalesced eigenstates under a tunable reciprocity-breaking perturbation remains less systematically explored. Here, we show that tunable nonreciprocal coupling can produce state-selective splitting of the coalesced eigenstates near a second-order polarization EP. Using temporal coupled-mode theory, we find that the corresponding off-diagonal perturbation produces a triangular Hamiltonian in the circular-polarization basis. In the ideal limit, one eigenstate remains pinned to the EP state, whereas the other is continuously reoriented by the perturbation. In a realistic scattering system, residual reverse-polarization conversion weakly displaces the nominally pinned branch, resulting in quasi-pinning. We numerically demonstrate this mechanism in a reflective magneto-optical metasurface supporting a circular-polarization EP of the reflection matrix near 582 nm. Full-wave simulations show that a perpendicular magneto-optical bias leaves one reflection eigenstate close to the EP state while reversibly displacing the other on the Poincare sphere. title: A library-based approach for inverse reconstruction of cavity depth using angle-resolved cathodoluminescence
summary: In nanofabrication processes, accurate metrology is a crucial step for obtaining control over the required critical dimensions in a device. Traditionally, scanning electron microscopy (SEM) is used to obtain high resolution measurements of the lateral dimension, but obtaining depth information on a thick sample is more complex. In this work, we use angle-resolved cathodoluminescence (AR-CL) spectroscopy to resolve this third dimension. Using 30 keV electrons in the SEM, CL is created at the bottom of a micrometer scale cavity milled in a gold surface. We show that reflections of the CL off the cavity sidewalls produce an interferogram which is a sensitive probe for the cavity geometry. The interferograms can be modelled using the finite-difference time-domain method, and we demonstrate that a neural network trained on a library of these simulated patterns can be used to reconstruct the cavity depth. This approach establishes a proof of concept for AR-CL based depth reconstruction within a prescribed geometry and could form a route towards advanced three-dimensional metrology of complex nanostructures.

AI.conclusion: AR-CL-based depth reconstruction is demonstrated as a proof of concept and could provide a route toward advanced three-dimensional metrology of complex nanostructures.

title: Topological terahertz fields from tunable vectorial currents
summary: Future information processing calls for photonic architectures with greater capacity, intrinsic resilience to noise, and direct integration with quantum materials and devices. Topological light pulses have recently emerged as promising candidates to meet these demands, yet the complexity underlying their unique properties also makes them challenging to generate, tune, and fully resolve in space and time. Here, we generate and actively tune topological light fields through transient vectorial currents in an optoelectronic metasurface. Incident linear polarization steers the local direction of photocurrents in graphene via nanoplasmonic resonators with triangular symmetry, while a global winding pattern enables continuous tuning between compressional and circulating charge flows. Under ultrafast excitation, these currents radiate single-cycle terahertz toroidal pulses spanning electric- and magnetic-dominant modes with dynamically evolving skyrmion textures. Full spatiotemporal mapping and reconstruction provide a complete visualization of the toroidal structure of light, directly tracing the closed field surfaces while continuously tracking skyrmion number and helicity throughout a single cycle. These results connect two-dimensional vectorial currents to rich three-dimensional electromagnetic field structures, while establishing a versatile integrated platform for higher-dimensional photonic information processing and emerging material spectroscopies.

title: Witnessing Gaussian Coexistence and Correlation-Ellipse Tomography
summary: Gaussian light is specified by second-order field moments, yet their hidden correlation geometry can demand higher-order intensity measurements. We establish a measurement hierarchy for "Gaussian coexistence", i.e., the simultaneous presence of cross covariance and cross pseudocovariance. For two zero-mean Gaussian modes with circular marginals, all unperturbed intensity moments of second or third order are blind to coexistence. In contrast, a balanced fourth-order residual provides a necessary and sufficient witness. Their identities, however, remain fundamentally ambiguous: recovering the two correlation strengths does not reveal which belongs to the covariance and which to the pseudocovariance. Unexpectedly, adding thermal fluctuations resolves this ambiguity: an independent, correlated thermal probe selectively modifies the covariance while leaving the pseudocovariance unchanged, allowing the two correlation strengths to be individually identified. Moreover, a coherent reference in only one arm then makes their relative phase accessible through third-order intensity correlation. Together, these measurements reconstruct a correlation ellipse and its Poincaré-sphere coordinates, determining the relative channel strengths and the ellipse orientation. The framework separates what intensity detection can witness, what thermal probing can identify, and what a single phase reference can orient, turning inaccessible Gaussian correlation structure into a quantitatively reconstructible geometry.

title: Propagation-tunable fractional Stokes skyrmions in conical refraction
summary: Conical refraction in a biaxial crystal generates Stokes textures whose finite-domain skyrmion number takes fractional values tunable through free-space propagation, while the underlying azimuthal winding remains unchanged. For a circularly polarised Gaussian input, the skyrmion number is governed by the boundary Stokes parameter, $N_\mathrm{sk}=[1-s_3(R_\mathrm{cut},Z)]/2$. Six-state polarimetry reveals fractional values of 0.523, 0.565 and 0.266 in the Lloyd, Poggendorff and Raman regions, respectively, in close agreement with Belsky-Khapalyuk-Berry predictions of 0.530, 0.550 and 0.250, and reproduces the predicted longitudinal evolution. Conical refraction thus provides a passive route to propagation-tunable fractional Stokes skyrmions, in which continuously evolving polarisation geometry coexists with a fixed topological winding.

title: Dynamic tuning of anisotropy-induced quasi-bound-states-in-the-continuum in liquid-crystal integrated dielectric metasurfaces
summary: Symmetry-protected quasi-bound states in the continuum (qBICs) in all-dielectric metasurfaces can be excited either by introducing a geometrical asymmetry into the unit cell or by illuminating the metasurface under oblique incidence. To date, tuning the coupling strength of such qBICs to the continuum has mainly relied on control of the geometrical asymmetry. Here, we show that qBICs can also be induced in a symmetric dielectric metasurface by embedding the latter into an anisotropic birefringent medium, and that they can be actively tuned by either rotating the anisotropy axis of the medium or by varying the degree of anisotropy. We experimentally implement a corresponding system by embedding a highly symmetric silicon nanocylinder metasurface into a nematic liquid crystal (LC) cell. Importantly, the LC does not only provide the desired birefringence, but also dynamic control of its strength as well as of the orientation of its anisotropy axis in response to different external stimuli. Specifically, applying voltage across the LC cell, where the LC molecules are pre-aligned along one of the lattice directions of the metasurface, enables out-of-plane rotation of the anisotropy axis of the LC medium. Meanwhile, its birefringence can be tuned by changing the temperature. In our experiments, the coupling of the qBICs to the radiation continuum is first maximized by the application of 25 V across the LC cell at room temperature. We then systematically tune the temperature and show that the resonance depth of the qBIC modes, which is associated with their coupling strength to the continuum, of the qBIC modes increases monotonously with birefringence. Our findings establish anisotropy-induced qBICs in LC integrated dielectric metasurfaces as a promising platform for actively reconfigurable metasurfaces and their applications in displays, optical modulation and tunable photonic devices.

AI.tldr: The paper demonstrates that quasi-bound states in the continuum can be induced in a symmetric all-dielectric metasurface by embedding it in an anisotropic birefringent liquid-crystal medium and actively tuned by rotating the anisotropy axis with voltage or changing the birefringence with temperature.

title: Quantum Tautochrone for photons and atoms
summary: The tautochrone problem, in which the travel time to a common point is independent of the starting position, has served as a foundational model in classical mechanics. Here we establish its quantum counterpart in engineered photonic waveguide arrays and atomic optical lattices, where nonuniform couplings drive photons and particles launched from different positions to converge simultaneously at a common site. Using higher-order correlation functions, we show that this quantum tautochrone effect holds for both bosons and fermions, with quantum statistics governing the character of the convergence: bosons converge onto the same site, while fermions, constrained by Pauli exclusion, gather at neighboring sites. For bosonic atoms, we further show how the tautochrone dynamics is shaped by lattice inhomogeneity, phase-space structure, and on-site interactions.

title: Magnetometry and slow light in PT-symmetric cavity optomechanics
summary: The generation of optical higher-order sidebands, which produces new frequencies with regular spectral separation, holds significant promise for applications in optical communication and quantum metrology. We investigate second-order sideband generation and tunable slow-fast light effects in a parity-time (PT)-symmetric cavity optomechanics and propose an enhanced magnetometer scheme. We demonstrate that the PT-symmetric structure, an external magnetic field, and the photon tunneling strength provide powerful and flexible control over both the second-order sideband efficiency, as well as the broadening and switching of slow-fast light propagation. Operating in the PT-symmetry-protected phases, our magnetometer based on the second-order sideband achieves a theoretical sensitivity at the picotesla level, surpassing the performance of previous optomechanical approaches. Our results offer new strategies for magnetic field sensing and optical transmission control, paving the way toward applications in quantum sensing and optical information storage.

title: Tweezing microparticles by tightly focused optical skyrmionic fields
summary: The concept of skyrmions, once translated to the optical domain, provides a topological framework to investigate structured light-matter interactions. However, their practical use for the manipulation of material systems remains barely explored. Here, we experimentally demonstrate trapping and tunable orbital motion of dielectric microparticles in tightly focused skyrmionic polarization textures prepared using a compact spin-orbit optical element. We explore the tweezing capabilities at fixed topology either by varying the relative weights of the orthogonally polarized components or by switching between skyrmion and bimeron polarization textures. Vectorial focusing and optical-force calculations qualitatively reproduce the experimental observations. These results motivate extending skyrmionic light to the manipulation of micro-objects, including birefringent and chiral samples.

title: Competing Symmetry Breakings and Spontaneous Parity Restoration in Desynchronously Pumped Kerr Resonators
summary: Symmetry breaking is a cornerstone of nonlinear science, where stronger driving typically compounds parity loss across coupled degrees of freedom. Here, we uncover a counterintuitive symmetry-restoring transition driven by the competition between internal spontaneous polarization symmetry breaking (PSB) and external explicit temporal symmetry breaking (TSB) in desynchronously pumped Kerr resonators. Tuning pump-cavity desynchronization steers dissipative cavity solitons from pure PSB, through a robust hybrid symmetry-breaking (HSB) regime where both asymmetries coexist, into a pure TSB state accompanied by the abrupt, spontaneous restoration of polarization parity. Using collective-coordinate perturbation theory, we map the effective Ginzburg-Landau potential landscape and show that kinematic drift weakens local driving until a saddle-node bifurcation eliminates the temporal confining barrier. Corroborated by full Ikeda-map simulations across the phase boundary, our results demonstrate how driven-dissipative systems sacrifice internal order to satisfy external kinematic constraints, offering a general paradigm for competing order parameters in multidimensional nonlinear systems.

title: Temporal Soliton Waves in Modern Fiber Laser Systems

title: Mechanisms of turnkey soliton generation in self-injection-locked photonic-crystal ring resonators
summary: Turnkey generation of dissipative Kerr solitons in photonic-crystal ring resonators relies on the interplay between engineered mode splitting, self-injection locking, and modulation instability, yet the mechanism governing soliton initiation and number selection remains incompletely understood. We investigate this interplay using coupled Lugiato-Lefever equations with a self-consistent nonlinear self-injection-locking condition. Analysis of continuous-wave steady states and their locking stability reveals operating points accessible through feedback-induced transitions between split resonances. Evaluating modulation-instability gain at these points identifies conditions for comb initiation and links the dominant unstable sideband modes to soliton-number selectivity. Direct time-domain simulations corroborate the analysis, showing that appropriately chosen mode splitting enables highly repeatable single-soliton generation without external laser-frequency scans. The final soliton number is nevertheless shaped by subsequent nonlinear evolution and feedback-induced detuning changes, rather than by the initial instability alone. We also show that larger dispersion suppresses higher-order unstable modes and favors lower soliton numbers.

title: Theory of modulation instability for coupled microresonators
summary: Thanks to hybridization phenomena, coupled microresonator systems enable modulation instability (MI) of the continuous wave background field across all possible dispersion combinations: anomalous-anomalous, normal-normal, and anomalous-normal microrings. Here, using the Lugiato-Lefever model in the supermode basis for two coupled microresonators with arbitrary second-order dispersion coefficients, arbitrary losses, and coupling strength, we derive a general eigenvalue problem for the $4\times 4$ matrix. We consider the regime of resonance splitting, in which the pump couples only to one of the two supermodes, allowing us to obtain analytical expressions for the stationary continuous-wave field distributed over the coupled system. When the microresonators have similar geometry, the antidiagonal elements of the eigenvalue-problem matrix nearly vanish, and we obtain a fully analytical solution for the MI gain rate for the entire range of coupled microresonator devices. Finally, we investigate cases in which the analytical treatment must be supplemented with more accurate numerical solutions of the MI eigenvalue problem, though even then the analytical theory captures the main features of the four-wave mixing process and the gain-rate behavior.

title: Phase matching of high-order harmonics driven by a combined coherent and bright squeezed vacuum field
summary: High-order harmonic generation (HHG) driven by non-classical light provides new insights into light-matter interactions and paves the way to quantum attosecond spectroscopy. Achieving phase matching is vital for generating bright HHG sources, while it has received comparatively limited attention in quantum-light-driven HHG. In this work, we investigate the phase matching of HHG driven by an intense coherent field combined with a weak bright squeezed vacuum (BSV) field, using a semiclassical ensemble of coherent-field realizations sampled from the Husimi-$Q$ probability distribution. We reveal the physical mechanism behind the distinct pressure dependence of the harmonic yields for odd, even and half-integer sidebands spectral components, as observed in our previous experiment [arXiv:2607.20941]. The simulations and phase-matching model demonstrate that the BSV-induced perturbation of the electron action phase could introduce an additional sub-cycle phase mismatch, such that the amplitude of sub-cycle bursts could be significantly modified by gas pressure after macroscopic propagation, even when the harmonic yield is near the optimum. The resulting amplitude asymmetry of sub-cycle bursts leads to a significant intensity contrast between half-integer sidebands harmonics, manifesting as distinct pressure dependence of their yields. Our findings reveal the phase-matching mechanism in two-color quantum-light-driven HHG, and suggest opportunities for macroscopic control of the non-classical HHG source.

title: Single-shot on-chip measurement of the modal Stokes parameters
summary: Integrated photonics has recently facilitated manipulating multimode partially coherent light in a compact mesh of Mach-Zehnder interferometers. A critical task in this context is on-chip reconstruction of the coherence matrix through a sequence of measurement configurations, thus giving rise to a speed bottleneck stemming from temporal delays in tuning on-chip phase shifts. Here we demonstrate single-shot reconstruction of the coherence matrix for two-mode partially coherent light by parallelizing the on-chip measurements of the modal Stokes parameters, thereby exchanging space for time. Although a larger chip area is required, the reconstruction is limited only by detection speed, thus potentially paving the way to real-time reconstruction of coherence matrices for applications in high-speed communications, cryptography, computation, and sensing.

AI.conclusion: Parallelized on-chip modal Stokes parameter measurements can remove the phase-tuning delay bottleneck in coherence-matrix reconstruction and potentially enable real-time reconstruction for high-speed communications, cryptography, computation, and sensing.

title: Supersymmetry of Helmholtz waves
summary: Symmetry organizes physical laws, links conservation principles to transformations, and reveals connections between seemingly different systems. We show that Helmholtz waves support Witten supersymmetry through their spatial symmetries, without additional internal degrees of freedom. Reflection across the transverse horizontal axis induces a $\mathbb{Z}_{2}$ grading of the Euclidean algebra, whose odd generators supply charges connecting opposite-parity Cartesian and Bessel modes at equal separation eigenvalues. The Bessel model has an unpaired even zero mode, Witten index one, and unbroken supersymmetry for any rotation-axis position along the reflection line. We express all four separators through mixed supercommutators of displaced orbital-angular-momentum generators, establish Weber pairing through a spectral sign operator, and identify the obstruction to equal-eigenvalue Mathieu pairing at nonzero ellipticity. We extend our construction to multiple transverse shells and generate supersymmetric partner fields with a common Talbot recurrence. Gaussian apodization centered on the rotation axis gives finite-power fields and preserves our charge relations during exact forward propagation while modifying the ideal revival. Our framework may guide optical transformations between parity partners and the characterization of structured fields.

title: Longitudinal-dither wavefront sensing: Calibration-free measurement of mode mismatch
summary: Mode mismatch between a gravitational-wave detector and the beams injected into it lowers the power stored in the arms and the level of squeezing. Correcting it requires the complex amplitudes of the three second-order modes, measured on a calibrated scale with the cavity on resonance at its operating power. Here we present a method that obtains a signal proportional to the mismatch by moving the beam on the wavefront sensors already used for alignment control. A longitudinal dither of the cavity adds to the resonant mode a reference field, which reaches the sensors through the same signal chains and so calibrates both the scale of this signal and the Gouy phases of the sensors and actuators, with no external calibration. We demonstrate the method on an optical cavity held on resonance in its operating state at input powers of 2 W and 62 W. At 2 W it yields an optical model that agrees with independent measurements in the mode content, and with the layout model in the actuator Gouy phase within its uncertainty of about $1^\circ$. At 62 W the thermally induced change of the eigenmode is decomposed into waist-size and waist-position changes. The method requires only components that every controlled cavity already possesses and enables continuous in situ monitoring of the mode matching in the operating state.

title: Recovery of Extended Modes from the Non-Hermitian Skin Effect Due to Local Nonlinearity on a Boundary
summary: Localization in continuum spectra known as the non-Hermitian skin effect is widely believed to be a consequence of nontrivial topology of bulk bands. However, the robustness of the non-Hermitian skin effect against nonlinear effects is still a nontrivial problem. We here reveal that single-bond nonlinearity on a boundary can recover extended modes in a non-Hermitian tight-binding model. We propose and analyze a one-dimensional minimal model, where we introduce a nonlinear phase shift of a hopping term only at boundary sites. We also propose a possible photonic setup to dynamically observe the nonlinearity-induced extended modes as a steady state. Our results thus challenge the conventional notion of the non-Hermitian skin effect by revealing its dependence on nonlinear boundary conditions.

title: Programmable multipartite entanglement analogues
summary: Quantum entanglement underpins the quantum information science. Its multipartite forms distribute coherence across several subsystems, but controlling their composition and order is increasingly difficult as more subsystems participate. Classical nonseparable waves provide accessible analogues of these structures, although existing implementations largely fix the participating degrees of freedom through their generating architectures. Here we overcome this constraint by making multipartiteness itself programmable in electromagnetic fields. A spatiotemporal metasurface reconfigures the identity and number of coherently linked state spaces independently across polarization, frequency, orbital angular momentum, wavevector direction, and orthogonal envelope modes. We realize complete Bell-like and Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger-like families from bipartite to five-partite order and exchange constituents at fixed order. To our knowledge, the five-partite state has the highest multipartite order experimentally realized in classical electromagnetic fields. These results establish the distribution of coherence across physical state spaces as a programmable property of classical waves and provide a platform for studying selected structures of multipartite quantum states without invoking quantum entanglement or nonlocality.

title: Observation of programmable spatiotemporal quantum-inspired bits
summary: Coherent superposition allows information to be encoded in the geometry of physical states1-7. Preparing individual states, however, does not determine how they can be organized throughout a wave, because the wave propagation and modulation constrain the underlying interference. Here we observe programmable spatiotemporal quantum-inspired bits in a space-time metasurface. Coherent synthesis from four discrete responses per polarization channel produces two-component states with the projective geometry of a pure quantum bit. Joint state-space synthesis retains the interference constraints of the shared waveform while allowing distinct polarization states to coexist at different resolved frequencies. Paired spatial and temporal codes organize these states into the prescribed trajectories, reconfigurable Stokes skyrmions and distinct polarizations at 48 experimentally resolved nonzero harmonic orders generated by a shared code pair. This connects the local state preparation to programmable field organization, establishing a physical basis for quantum-inspired information carriers whose encoding can exploit the geometrical paths, spatial winding and coordinated spectral states.

title: Electrons in a hard-wall cylinder with helicoidal metric: time-reversal pairing, cubic anticrossings, and twist-activated dipole transitions
comment: 26 pages, 17 figures, 8 tables. Corrects the analysis of E. O. Silva, Opt. Quantum Electron. 58, 113 (2026), doi:10.1007/s11082-026-08693-8, whose retraction has been requested. Scripts and verification tests are provided as ancillary files
summary: We study the scalar Schrödinger equation in a helicoidal metric when the axial direction is closed by Dirichlet walls built into the operator domain. With hard walls, the axial derivative cannot be replaced by a traveling-wave factor, and in a rotationally symmetric spinless cavity, time reversal makes the levels with azimuthal numbers $m$ and $-m$ exactly degenerate. We write the Hamiltonian as a Hermitian coupled-subband matrix and give an exact gauge-adapted variational representation. For a finite radius, the leading twist correction is quadratic, and changes sign at a critical aspect ratio; for an unbounded radial domain, it is linear in $|Ω_g|$. Retuning the aspect ratio through an isolated radial--axial resonance within one $m$ sector opens an avoided crossing with gap $Δ_{\mathrm{gap}}/E_R=1.648775\ldots|Ω_gR^2/L|^3$ to leading order. A transverse dipole transition forbidden without twist acquires an oscillator strength quadratic in the twist, with leading coefficient $0.0559408010$ for $R/L=2$ from perturbation theory. Dipole sum rules and the convergence of the currents serve as checks on the numerics. We also give the inverse-mass tensor required for a scalar realization and re-examine each statement and figure of the earlier article [Opt. Quantum Electron. \textbf{58}, 113 (2026)] within the corrected model.

title: Reconfigurable Chiral Phonons and Their Selection in Asymmetrically Stacked Graphene MoirMoiré Superlattices
summary: Chiral phonons, lattice vibrations carrying angular momentum, offer a new handle for controlling phonon-mediated phenomena in condensed matter, yet their on-demand generation and deterministic control remain challenging. Here we show, using helicity-resolved Raman spectroscopy, that asymmetrically stacked graphene moiré superlattices provide a reconfigurable platform for chiral phonons. We observe a finite degree of circular polarization for both chiral interlayer shear phonons and intralayer optical phonons. A chiral-phonon Raman-tensor model attributes this response to interfacial $C_{2}$-symmetry breaking together with Raman resonance within the van Hove singularity region. Reversing either the twist sense or the stacking order inverts the degree of circular polarization through the spatial transformations linking the corresponding stacking geometries. By tuning the excitation energy and twist angle, we achieve nearly full-range control of the degree of circular polarization of interlayer shear phonons, from $-1$ to $1$, while gate-induced interlayer potential redistribution enables substantial and reversible in situ modulation. title: Spatial switching near a four-loop homoclinic bouquet: a mechanism for multi-bump bound states in coupled nonlinear Schrödinger systems
summary: We study how a localized standing wave of a coupled nonlinear Schrödinger (CNLS) system can switch between components from one pulse to the next. Apart from trajectories asymptotic to the saddle in the corresponding time direction, these manifolds characterize one-sided trapping near the bouquet within the critical Hamiltonian level, namely the level set containing the saddle equilibrium. Both manifolds have codimension one in this level. We prove that if they intersect transversely away from the bouquet, producing super-homoclinic orbits, then there exist infinitely many multi-bump homoclinic orbits to the saddle. These orbits correspond to multi-bump localized standing waves of the CNLS system.

title: Density-dependent photocarrier recombination in $γ$-InSe
summary: We studied the photocarrier dynamics in $γ$-InSe using femtosecond transient reflectance spectroscopy. By measuring the dependence of the differential reflectance on the injected carrier density, we established an empirical relation between the optical response and carrier density, allowing quantitative analysis of the recombination dynamics. At high carrier densities, the dynamics are dominated by a second-order recombination process, with a rate constant of $3.8\times10^{-6}~\mathrm{cm^3\,s^{-1}}$. At low densities, the decay becomes approximately exponential, with a carrier lifetime of about 7 ps. We also resolved an initial rise of the band-edge response with a time constant of less than 1 ps, which is attributed to hot-carrier cooling. These results reveal the competition between first-order and second-order recombination in $γ$-InSe and provide quantitative insights into its ultrafast photocarrier dynamics.

title: Non-integer high harmonic generation from many-body nonadiabatic gating
comment: 10 pages main text, 5 figures, 43 pages supplementary information
summary: High harmonic generation (HHG) in solids typically produces a rigid frequency comb locked to exact integer multiples of the drive photon energy. In strongly correlated materials, however, the light field can dynamically transform the electronic state on the timescale of harmonic generation itself, potentially violating this rule. Here, we report giant blueshifted, non-integer HHG in a cuprate Mott insulator Sr$_2$CuO$_3$ produced by mid-infrared excitations. Concurrent transient reflectivity measurements and time-dependent exact-diagonalization simulations of a driven Hubbard model support a many-body temporal gating mechanism that suppresses light emission on the trailing edge of the pulse, thereby blueshifting radiated harmonics in the frequency domain. Our findings establish HHG emission energy as a sensitive probe of quantum many-body dynamics and pave the way for exploration and manipulation of correlated electronic phases of matter with strong-field spectroscopy.

title: Beyond Quantum Mechanics: From Nonlinear to Emergent and Solitonic Approaches
comment: Master's thesis in Physics, Sapienza University of Rome, defended on 17 November 2026. Supervisor: Prof. Claudio Conti. 137 pages
summary:
This thesis investigates the role of nonlinearity in approaches beyond standard quantum mechanics, following a path from modifications of quantum dynamics to the possibility of an emergent statistical description. We first examine Weinberg's nonlinear formulation and its implications for the statistical interpretation of quantum states. We then discuss de Broglie-Bohm theory and the Madelung formulation, which provide a framework for comparing guided trajectories with ensemble descriptions involving momentum fluctuations. The Hall-Reginatto exact uncertainty approach identifies the fluctuation energy associated with the quantum potential.
  We then investigate whether quantum dynamics can emerge from the collective statistics of solitons in a fluctuating background, using a Galilean formulation of the complex sine-Gordon model. Within a weak-noise approximation, we identify a regime in which the statistics of the soliton centres reproduce the Schr{ö}dinger equation, with an effective action scale determined by the background fluctuations. This correspondence is established for Gaussian ensembles and potentials at most quadratic.
  These results provide a concrete setting for exploring how quantum dynamics can emerge as a statistical description of underlying nonlinear field dynamics.

title: Whistler instability driven by electron trapping in magnetic dips
summary: Using fully kinetic particle-in-cell simulations, we show how free energy released by an ion-scale instability reaches electron scales through its effect on the electron distribution. Electrons trapped in these dips develop an enhanced temperature anisotropy and butterfly-shaped distributions, similar to those observed by spacecraft in the Earth's magnetosheath. By tracking the energy transfer in velocity space, we show that the gradients created by trapping drive whistler waves through cyclotron resonance. The whistlers in turn scatter the electrons in pitch angle, flattening velocity-space gradients and heating the electrons along the magnetic field. As a result, the electron anisotropy drops to about half of the double-adiabatic prediction once the whistler power peaks. Our results show that it is the shape of the electron distribution in magnetic dips, rather than its temperature anisotropy alone, that drives the whistlers.

title: Annular-curvature effects on high-frequency azimuthal fluctuations in 3D PIC simulations of Hall-thruster plasmas
summary: Azimuthal instabilities and associated plasma fluctuations play an important role in anomalous cross-field electron transport in Hall thrusters. At rmin = 10 cm and 2 cm, the outer-channel electric-field amplitudes in the dominant wavenumber band exceed the inner-channel values by 26% and 53%, respectively. Density-electric-field covariance is preferentially concentrated in the outer channel and inner plume, with outer-to-inner magnitude ratios of 2.71 and 0.58 at rmin = 2 cm.
